## 1. Exposition of Singletons
There are six designations: the designation of aggregates (khandha-paññatti), the designation of bases (āyatana-paññatti), the designation of elements (dhātu-paññatti), the designation of truths (sacca-paññatti), the designation of faculties (indriya-paññatti), and the designation of individuals (puggala-paññatti).

To what extent is there a designation of aggregates for the aggregates? As far as the five aggregates—namely, the aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandha), the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), and the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha)—to that extent there is a designation of aggregates for the aggregates.

To what extent is there a designation of bases for the bases? As far as the twelve bases—namely, the eye-base, the object-base, the ear-base, the sound-base, the nose-base, the odor-base, the tongue-base, the taste-base, the body-base, the tangible-base, the mind-base, and the mental-object-base—to that extent there is a designation of bases for the bases.

To what extent is there a designation of elements for the elements? As far as the eighteen elements—namely, the eye-element, the visible-object-element, the eye-consciousness-element, the ear-element, the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, the nose-element, the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, the tongue-element, the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, the body-element, the tangible-object-element, the body-consciousness-element, the mind-element, the mental-object-element, and the mind-consciousness-element—to that extent there is a designation of elements for the elements.
102:
To what extent is there the designation of truths for the truths? As far as the four truths—namely, the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca), the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca), the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca), and the truth of the path (magga-sacca)—to this extent is there the designation of truths for the truths.

To what extent is there the designation of faculties for the faculties? As far as the twenty-two faculties—namely, the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the female-faculty, the male-faculty, the life-faculty, the pleasure-faculty, the pain-faculty, the joy-faculty, the grief-faculty, the equanimity-faculty, the faith-faculty, the energy-faculty, the mindfulness-faculty, the concentration-faculty, the wisdom-faculty, the I-shall-know-the-unknown-faculty, the knowledge-faculty, and the one-who-has-known-faculty—to this extent is there the designation of faculties for the faculties.

## Exposition

## 1. Designation of Single Persons

Who is the person liberated temporarily (samayavimutta)? Here, a certain person from time to time, from occasion to occasion, dwells having touched the eight liberations with the mental body, and having seen them with wisdom, some of his taints are exhausted—this person is called "liberated temporarily."

Who is the person liberated non-temporarily (asamayavimutta)? Here, a certain person does not dwell from time to time, from occasion to occasion, having touched the eight liberations with the mental body, but having seen them with wisdom, his taints are exhausted—this person is called "liberated non-temporarily." All noble persons are non-temporarily liberated in regard to the noble liberations.

Who is the person liable to fall away (kuppadhamma)? Here, a certain person is an obtainer of the attainments of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere. However, he is not one who obtains them at will, not one who obtains them without difficulty, not one who obtains them without effort. He cannot enter into or emerge from whatever attainment he wishes, wherever he wishes, for as long as he wishes. There is the possibility that, due to negligence, those attainments of that person might fall away—this person is called "liable to fall away."

Who is the person not liable to fall away (akuppadhamma)? Here, a certain person is an obtainer of the attainments of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere. He is one who obtains them at will, obtains them without difficulty, obtains them without effort. He can enter into and emerge from whatever attainment he wishes, wherever he wishes, for as long as he wishes. There is no possibility, no occasion, that due to negligence, those attainments of that person might fall away—this person is called "not liable to fall away." All noble persons are not liable to fall away in regard to the noble liberations.

Who is the person of the nature of falling away (parihānadhamma)? Here, a certain person is an obtainer of the attainments of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere. However, he is not one who obtains them at will, not one who obtains them without difficulty, not one who obtains them without effort...
115:
...he cannot enter into or emerge from whatever attainment he wishes, wherever he wishes, for as long as he wishes. There is the possibility that, due to negligence, that person might fall away from those attainments. This person is called "one of the nature of falling away (parihānadhamma)."

Who is the person not of the nature of falling away (aparihānadhamma)? Here, a certain person is an obtainer of the attainments of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere. He is one who obtains them at will, obtains them without difficulty, obtains them without effort. He can enter into and emerge from whatever attainment he wishes, wherever he wishes, for as long as he wishes. There is no possibility, no occasion, that due to negligence, that person might fall away from those attainments. This person is called "one not of the nature of falling away (aparihānadhamma)." All noble persons are not of the nature of falling away in regard to the noble liberations.

Who is the person able through volition (cetanābhabba)? Here, a certain person is an obtainer of the attainments of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere. He is not one who obtains them at will, not one who obtains them without difficulty, not one who obtains them without effort. He cannot enter into or emerge from whatever attainment he wishes, wherever he wishes, for as long as he wishes. If he repeatedly exerts volition and effort to enter the attainment, he does not fall away from those attainments. If he does not repeatedly exert volition and effort, he falls away from those attainments. This person is called "one able through volition (cetanābhabba)."

Who is the person able through guarding (anurakkhaṇābhabba)? Here, a certain person is an obtainer of the attainments of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere. He is not one who obtains them at will, not one who obtains them without difficulty, not one who obtains them without effort. He cannot enter into or emerge from whatever attainment he wishes, wherever he wishes, for as long as he wishes. If he repeatedly guards [his attainments], he does not fall away from those attainments. If he does not repeatedly guard them, he falls away from those attainments. This person is called "one able through guarding (anurakkhaṇābhabba)."

Who is the person who is a worldling (puthujjana)? The person in whom the three fetters have not yet been abandoned, and who does not practice for the sake of abandoning those states—this person is called a "worldling (puthujjana)."

Who is the person who has entered the lineage (gotrabhū)? The person who is possessed of those states immediately after which the descent into the noble state occurs—this person is called "one who has entered the lineage (gotrabhū)."
116:
Who is the person restrained by fear? The seven types of trainees (sekhas) and virtuous worldlings (puthujjanas) are those restrained by fear. An Arahant is not a person restrained by fear.

Who is the person incapable of progress? Those persons who are possessed of the obstruction of kamma (ānantariya-kamma), possessed of the obstruction of defilement (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi), possessed of the obstruction of result (ahetu or dvihetu rebirth), who lack faith, lack desire (to do good), lack wisdom, are foolish and dull, and are incapable of entering the right path of assurance (magga-niyāma) in wholesome states—these are called persons "incapable of progress."

Who is the person capable of progress? Those persons who are not possessed of the obstruction of kamma, not possessed of the obstruction of defilement, not possessed of the obstruction of result, who have faith, have desire, have wisdom, are not foolish and dull, and are capable of entering the right path of assurance in wholesome states—these are called persons "capable of progress."

Who is the person who is fixed? The five persons who have committed the deeds with immediate result (ānantariya-kamma) and those with fixed wrong view are fixed (in their destination to hell). The eight noble persons (ariya-puggalas) are also fixed (in their attainment of the path and fruit). Other persons are not fixed.

Who is the person practicing? The four persons possessed of the path are those practicing. The four persons possessed of the fruit are those established in the fruit.

Who is the person who is a "samasīsī" (one who attains simultaneously)? For whichever person the exhaustion of taints (āsavas) and the end of life occur simultaneously, neither before nor after the other—this person is called a "samasīsī."

Who is the person who stays for an aeon (ṭhitakappī)? If a person were practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, and it were the time for the aeon to be consumed by fire, the aeon would not be consumed as long as that person has not realized the fruit of stream-entry. This person is called a "ṭhitakappī." All persons possessed of the path are ṭhitakappīs.

Who is the noble person (ariya)? The eight noble persons are the Ariyas. The remaining persons are non-Ariyas.
117:
What kind of person is a trainee (sekha)? The four persons possessed of the path and the three persons possessed of the (lower) fruits are called "trainees." An Arahant is one beyond training (asekha). The remaining persons are neither trainees nor those beyond training.

What kind of person is one with threefold knowledge (tevijja)? A person possessed of the three knowledges is called "one with threefold knowledge."

What kind of person is one with six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiñña)? A person possessed of the six supernormal powers is called "one with six supernormal powers."

What kind of person is a Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha)? Here, a certain person, in regard to teachings not heard before, realizes the Four Noble Truths by himself, and in those truths attains omniscience and mastery over the powers. This person is called a "Fully Enlightened One."

What kind of person is a Solitary Enlightened One (Paccekasambuddha)? Here, a certain person, in regard to teachings not heard before, realizes the Four Noble Truths by himself, but does not attain omniscience in those truths, nor mastery over the powers. This person is called a "Solitary Enlightened One."

What kind of person is one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta)? Here, a certain person dwells having touched the eight liberations with his mental body, and having seen with wisdom, his taints are exhausted. This person is called "one liberated in both ways."

What kind of person is one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta)? Here, a certain person does not dwell having touched the eight liberations with his mental body, but having seen with wisdom, his taints are exhausted. This person is called "one liberated by wisdom."

What kind of person is a body-witness (kāyasakkhī)? Here, a certain person dwells having touched the eight liberations with his mental body, and having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are exhausted. This person is called a "body-witness."

What kind of person is one who has attained through vision (diṭṭhippatta)? Here, a certain person understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." The [teachings] proclaimed by the Tathāgata...
118:
That person has clearly seen and thoroughly penetrated with wisdom the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata. Having seen with wisdom, some of his taints (āsavas) are exhausted. This person is called 'one attained to vision' (diṭṭhippatta).

Who is the person liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta)? Here, a certain person understands as it really is: 'This is suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.' He has clearly seen and thoroughly penetrated with wisdom the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata. Having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are exhausted, but not in the same way as the one attained to vision. This person is called 'one liberated by faith' (saddhāvimutta).

Who is the Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī)? For a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, the faculty of wisdom is predominant; he develops the noble path led by wisdom, preceded by wisdom. This person is called a 'Dhamma-follower' (dhammānusārī). A person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry is a Dhamma-follower; when standing in the fruit, he is one attained to vision.

Who is the faith-follower (saddhānusārī)? For a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, the faculty of faith is predominant; he develops the noble path led by faith, preceded by faith. This person is called a 'faith-follower' (saddhānusārī). A person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry is a faith-follower; when standing in the fruit, he is one liberated by faith.

Who is the person with seven births at most (sattakkhattuparama)? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the three fetters, is a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. Having wandered and roamed through the worlds of gods and humans for seven times at most, he makes an end of suffering. This person is called 'one with seven births at most' (sattakkhattuparama).

Who is the person going from family to family (kolaṅkola)? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the three fetters, is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds...
119:
...fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination (is a stream-enterer). Having wandered and roamed through two or three families, he makes an end of suffering. This person is called 'one going from family to family' (kolaṅkola).

What kind of person is a one-seeder (ekabījī)? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the three fetters, is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. Having been reborn in only one human existence, he makes an end of suffering. This person is called a 'one-seeder' (ekabījī).

What kind of person is a once-returner (sakadāgāmī)? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the three fetters and the weakening of greed, hatred, and delusion, is a once-returner. Having come back to this world only once, he makes an end of suffering. This person is called a 'once-returner' (sakadāgāmī).

What kind of person is a non-returner (anāgāmī)? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth (a Brahma). He is one who attains Nibbāna there, not being subject to return from that world. This person is called a 'non-returner' (anāgāmī).

What kind of person is one who attains Nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī)? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth. He is one who attains Nibbāna there, not being subject to return from that world. Immediately upon being reborn, or before reaching the middle of his lifespan, he generates the noble path for the abandoning of the higher fetters. This person is called 'one who attains Nibbāna in the interval' (antarāparinibbāyī).

What kind of person is one who attains Nibbāna upon landing (upahaccaparinibbāyī)? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth. He is one who attains Nibbāna there, not being subject to return from that world. Having passed the middle of his lifespan, or when approaching the time of death, he generates the noble path for the abandoning of the higher fetters. This person is called 'one who attains Nibbāna upon landing' (upahaccaparinibbāyī).

What kind of person is one who attains Nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī)? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth. In that Brahma realm...
120: ...(in that realm) he is one who attains Nibbāna, one who is not subject to return from that world. That person, without the exertion of prompting through insight-knowledge, brings into being the Noble Path for the abandoning of the higher fetters—this person is called 'one who attains Nibbāna without exertion' (asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī). Who is the person who attains Nibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī)? Here, a certain person, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth; in that realm he attains Nibbāna, not subject to return from that world. That person, with the exertion of prompting through insight-knowledge, brings into being the Noble Path for the abandoning of the higher fetters—this person is called 'one who attains Nibbāna with exertion' (sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī). Who is the person who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī)? Here, a certain person, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth; in that realm he attains Nibbāna, not subject to return from that world. Having passed away from the Aviha realm, he goes to the Atappa realm; having passed away from the Atappa realm, he goes to the Sudassa realm; having passed away from the Sudassa realm, he goes to the Sudassī realm; having passed away from the Sudassī realm, he goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm. In the Akaniṭṭha realm, he brings into being the Noble Path for the abandoning of the higher fetters—this person is called 'one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm' (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī). Who is the person who is a stream-enterer (sotāpanno) and the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry? The person practicing for the abandoning of the three fetters is the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. The person for whom the three fetters have been abandoned—this person is called a 'stream-enterer' (sotāpanno). The person practicing for the attenuation of sensual lust and ill will is the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning. The person for whom sensual lust and ill will have been attenuated—this person is called a 'once-returner' (sakadāgāmī). The person practicing for the total abandoning of sensual lust and ill will is the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning. The person for whom sensual lust and ill will have been totally abandoned—this person is called a 'non-returner' (anāgāmī). The person practicing for the total abandoning of lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance is the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Arahantship. The person for whom...
121:
The person who has abandoned lust for fine-material existence, lust for formless existence, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance without remainder is called an "Arahant."

## The Exposition of the Groups of One (Ekakaniddesa) is concluded.

## 2. Designation of Individuals by Groups of Two (Dukapuggalapaññatti)

Who is the person who is angry? In that context, what is anger (kodha)? That which is anger, being angry, the state of being angry, hatred, hating, the state of being hateful, ill-will, malevolence, the state of being malevolent, hostility, opposition, ferocity, abruptness, and discontent of mind—this is called anger. The person in whom this anger is not abandoned is called an "angry person."

Who is the person who is malicious? In that context, what is malice (upanāha)? Anger in the preceding period is malice in the subsequent period. Such malice, harboring malice, the state of harboring malice, fixing, staying, establishing, repeatedly pursuing, binding, and making anger firm—this is called malice. The person in whom this malice is not abandoned is called a "malicious person."

Who is the person who is a denigrator? In that context, what is denigration (makkha)? That which is denigration, denigrating, the state of being a denigrator, harshness, and the act of harshness—this is called denigration. The person in whom this denigration is not abandoned is called a "denigrator."

Who is the person who is domineering? In that context, what is domineering (paḷāsa)? That which is domineering, the state of being domineering, carrying out domineering, a ground for dispute, assuming equality, and not relinquishing—this is called domineering. The person in whom this domineering is not abandoned is called a "domineering person."
122:
Who is the envious person? In that term (issukī), what is envy (issā)? Envy, the state of being envious, jealousy, the state of being jealous, regarding the gain, honor, respect, esteem, salutation, and veneration of others—this is called envy (issā). The person in whom this envy is not abandoned is called an "envious person."

Who is the stingy person? In that term (maccharī), what is stinginess (macchariya)? There are five types of stinginess: stinginess regarding dwelling, stinginess regarding family, stinginess regarding gain, stinginess regarding status, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma. Such stinginess, the state of being stingy, the shrinking of the mind, miserliness, harshness, the mind's holding fast—this is called stinginess (macchariya). The person in whom this stinginess is not abandoned is called a "stingy person."

Who is the deceitful person? In that term (saṭho), what is deceit (sāṭheyya)? Here, a certain person is deceitful, extremely deceitful. That person's deceit, the state of being deceitful, harshness, concealment, the state of being concealed—this is called deceit (sāṭheyya). The person in whom this deceit is not abandoned is called a "deceitful person."

Who is the hypocritical person? In that term (māyāvī), what is hypocrisy (māyā)? Here, a certain person, having committed misconduct by body, having committed misconduct by speech, and having committed misconduct by mind, for the sake of concealing that misconduct, harbors an evil desire: "May others not know me." He desires, "May others not know me"; he intends, "May others not know me"; he speaks, "May others not know me"; he strives with the body, "May others not know me." Such hypocrisy, the state of being hypocritical, extreme trickery, deception, craftiness, covering, concealing, well-concealing, closing off, well-closing off, making obscure, making unrevealed, shrouding, an evil action—this is called hypocrisy (māyā). The person in whom this hypocrisy is not abandoned is called a "hypocritical person."

Who is the shameless person? In that term (ahiriko), what is shamelessness (ahirika)? Not being ashamed of what one should be ashamed of, not being ashamed of the commission of evil, unwholesome states—this is called shamelessness (ahirika). The person endowed with this shamelessness is called a "shameless person."
123:
Who is the person who lacks moral dread? In that context, what is the lack of moral dread (anottappa)? Not fearing the danger that should be feared due to the commission of evil, unwholesome states—this is called the lack of moral dread (anottappa). The person endowed with this lack of moral dread is called "one who lacks moral dread" (anottappī).

Who is the person who is difficult to admonish? In that context, what is intractability (dovacassatā)? When being spoken to in accordance with the Dhamma, the state of being difficult to speak to, the state of being oppositional, the state of delighting in opposition, lack of respect, the state of being disrespectful, lack of reverence, and lack of obedience—this is called intractability (dovacassatā). The person endowed with this intractability is called "one who is difficult to admonish" (dubbaco).

Who is the person with bad friends? In that context, what is bad friendship (pāpamittatā)? Associating with, frequenting, repeatedly associating with, serving, repeatedly serving, being devoted to, being extremely devoted to, and following the wishes of those persons who lack faith, lack virtue, have little learning, are stingy, and lack wisdom—this is called bad friendship (pāpamittatā). The person endowed with this bad friendship is called "one with bad friends" (pāpamitto).

Who is the person with unguarded sense doors? In that context, what is the state of having unguarded sense doors (indriyesu aguttadvāratā)? Here, a certain person, having seen a form with the eye, grasps at its signs (nimitta) and grasps at its details (anubyañjana). Because he dwells without restraining the eye-faculty, evil unwholesome states of covetousness (abhijjhā) and grief (domanassa) might follow and flow into him; he does not practice for the restraint of that eye-faculty, he does not guard the eye-faculty, he does not achieve restraint over the eye-faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear... [pe]... having smelled an odor with the nose... [pe]... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... [pe]... having touched a tangible object with the body... [pe]... having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he grasps at its signs and grasps at its details. Because he dwells without restraining the mind-faculty, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might follow and flow into him; he does not practice for the restraint of that mind-faculty, he does not guard the mind-faculty, he does not achieve restraint over the mind-faculty. This lack of guarding, lack of protection, lack of watchfulness, and lack of restraint over these six faculties—this is called the state of having unguarded sense doors (indriyesu aguttadvāratā). The person endowed with this state of having unguarded sense doors is called "one with unguarded sense doors" (indriyesu aguttadvāro).

Who is the person who is immoderate in eating? In that context, what is immoderation in eating (bhojane amattaññutā)? Here, a certain person, without reflection and without wise attention...
124:
... eats food for the sake of play, for intoxication, for adornment, and for beautification. In that regard, lack of contentment, lack of moderation, and eating without reflection is called immoderation in eating (bhojane amattaññutā). A person possessed of this immoderation in eating is called "one who is immoderate in eating."

Who is the person who is unmindful (muṭṭhassatī)? In that regard, what is unmindfulness (muṭṭhassacca)? That which is lack of mindfulness, lack of repeated recollection, lack of remembrance, non-recollection, non-remembrance, inability to retain, drifting of mindfulness, and forgetfulness—this is called unmindfulness. A person possessed of this unmindfulness is called "one who is unmindful."

Who is the person who lacks clear comprehension (asampajāno)? In that regard, what is lack of clear comprehension (asampajañña)? That which is non-knowing, non-seeing, non-realization of the Four Noble Truths, lack of repeated understanding, lack of full awakening, non-penetration, non-grasping, non-plunging into, non-observation, non-reflection, non-realization, lack of wisdom, foolishness, lack of clear comprehension, delusion, intense bewilderment, confusion, ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the underlying tendency of ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the barrier of ignorance, and the unwholesome root of delusion—this is called lack of clear comprehension. A person possessed of this lack of clear comprehension is called "one who lacks clear comprehension."

Who is the person who is deficient in virtue (sīlavipanno)? In that regard, what is deficiency in virtue (sīlavipatti)? Bodily transgression, verbal transgression, or both bodily and verbal transgression—this is called deficiency in virtue. All immorality is also called deficiency in virtue. A person possessed of this deficiency in virtue is called "one who is deficient in virtue."

Who is the person who is deficient in view (diṭṭhivipanno)? In that regard, what is deficiency in view (diṭṭhivipatti)? It is the view: "There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good or bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously reborn beings; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins who have attained the right path and practiced rightly, who proclaim this world and the other world having realized them for themselves by direct knowledge." Such a wrong view, a resort of views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views, a seizing, a grasping, an adherence, a misinterpretation, a wrong path, a bad way, wrongness, a sectarian landing-place, a perverted grasp...
125:
This is called deficiency in view (diṭṭhivipatti). All wrong views are also deficiency in view. A person possessed of this deficiency in view is called "one who is deficient in view" (diṭṭhivipanno).

What kind of person is one with internal fetters (ajjhattasaṃyojano)? The person for whom the five lower fetters pertaining to the sense sphere have not been abandoned—this person is called "one with internal fetters."

What kind of person is one with external fetters (bahiddhāsaṃyojano)? The person for whom the five higher fetters have not been abandoned—this person is called "one with external fetters."

What kind of person is one who is not angry (akkodhano)? In those states, what is anger (kodha)? Anger, the state of being angry, resentment, the state of being resentful, hostility, the state of being hostile, opposition, fierce opposition, churlishness, and the mind's lack of satisfaction—this is called anger. The person for whom this anger has been abandoned—this person is called "one who is not angry."

What kind of person is one who does not bear a grudge (anupanāhī)? In those states, what is bearing a grudge (upanāha)? Anger (kodha) occurs in the initial period, and bearing a grudge (upanāha) occurs in the subsequent period. Such bearing a grudge, the state of bearing a grudge, repeated establishing, firm establishing, following and binding, and the making firm of anger—this is called bearing a grudge. The person for whom this bearing a grudge has been abandoned—this person is called "one who does not bear a grudge."

What kind of person is one who is not a denigrator (amakkhī)? In those states, what is denigration (makkha)? Denigration, the state of being a denigrator, harshness, and the act of harshness—this is called denigration. The person for whom this denigration has been abandoned—this person is called "one who is not a denigrator."

What kind of person is one who is not spiteful (apaḷāsī)? In those states, what is spite (paḷāsa)? Spite, the state of being spiteful, the carrying of spite, the ground for dispute, rivalry, and not relinquishing one's view—this is called spite. The person for whom this spite has been abandoned—this person is called "one who is not spiteful."
126:
What kind of person is one who is not envious (anissukī)? In this context, what is envy (issā)? Envy, being envious, the state of being envious, jealousy, being jealous, the state of being jealous regarding the gains, hospitality, respect, esteem, salutation, and offerings of others—this is called envy. The person in whom this envy is abandoned is called 'one who is not envious.'

What kind of person is one who is not stingy (amaccharī)? In this context, what is stinginess (macchariya)? There are five types of stinginess: stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding beauty or fame, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma. Such stinginess, being stingy, the state of being stingy, selfishness, niggardliness, extreme stinginess, the state of the mind being held fast—this is called stinginess. The person in whom this stinginess is abandoned is called 'one who is not stingy.'

What kind of person is one who is not crafty (asaṭho)? In this context, what is craftiness (sāṭheyya)? Here, a certain person is crafty, very crafty. In this context, craftiness, being crafty, the state of being crafty, crookedness, being crooked, concealment, extreme concealment—this is called craftiness. The person in whom this craftiness is abandoned is called 'one who is not crafty.'

What kind of person is one who is not fraudulent (amāyāvī)? In this context, what is fraud (māyā)? Here, a certain person, having committed misconduct by body, having committed misconduct by speech, and having committed misconduct by mind, for the sake of concealing that misconduct, harbors an evil desire: 'May others not know me,' he desires; 'May others not know me,' he intends; 'May others not know me,' he speaks; 'May others not know me,' he strives with his body. Such fraud, being fraudulent, extreme deception, trickery, craftiness, scattering, concealment, thorough concealment, closing off, thorough closing off, making obscure, making unmanifest, hiding, the doing of evil—this is called fraud. The person in whom this fraud is abandoned is called 'one who is not fraudulent.'

What kind of person is one who is conscientious (hirimā)? In this context, what is moral shame (hiri)? That which is ashamed, being ashamed of what one should be ashamed of, being ashamed of the commission of evil, unwholesome states—this is called moral shame. A person endowed with this moral shame is called 'one who is conscientious.'

What kind of person is one who is scrupulous (ottappī)? In this context, what is moral dread (ottappa)? That which dreads, dreading what one should dread, dreading the commission of evil, unwholesome states—this is called moral dread. A person endowed with this moral dread is called 'one who is scrupulous.'
127:
What kind of person is one who is easy to admonish (suvaco)? What is amenability (sovacassatā)? When being spoken to by fellow practitioners of the Dhamma (regarding a fault), there is amenability, the state of being amenable, the nature of being amenable, the state of not taking it in a hostile way, the state of not being oppositional, respectfulness, the nature of being respectful, the state of having reverence, the state of being deferential—this is called amenability. A person endowed with this amenability is called 'one who is easy to admonish.'

What kind of person is one who has good friends (kalyāṇamitto)? What is good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā)? There are those persons who possess faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Associating with them, repeatedly associating with them, associating closely with them, attending on them, attending on them closely, devotion, great devotion, being inclined towards them—this is called good friendship. A person endowed with this good friendship is called 'one who has good friends.'

What kind of person is one who is guarded in the sense doors (indriyesu guttadvāro)? What is the state of being guarded in the sense doors (indriyesu guttadvāratā)? In this Dispensation, a certain person, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs or its secondary features. Since evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might follow him if he lived with the eye faculty unrestrained, he practices for its restraint, he guards the eye faculty, and he undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear... (pe)... Having smelled an odor with the nose... (pe)... Having tasted a flavor with the tongue... (pe)... Having felt a tangible object with the body... (pe)... Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or its secondary features. Since evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might follow him if he lived with the mind faculty unrestrained, he practices for its restraint, he guards the mind faculty, and he undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty. The guarding, protecting, watching over, and restraining of these six sense faculties—this is called the state of being guarded in the sense doors. A person endowed with this state of being guarded in the sense doors is called 'one who is guarded in the sense doors.'

What kind of person is one who is moderate in eating (bhojane mattaññū)? What is moderation in eating (bhojane mattaññutā)? In this Dispensation, a certain person partakes of food reflecting wisely: 'Not for fun, not for intoxication, not for ornament, not for beautification, but only for the maintenance and nourishment of this body, for its endurance, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life. Thus I shall terminate old feelings and not produce new feelings, and I shall have sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.' In that context, whatever state of contentment there is...
128:
There is moderation in eating through reflection. This state is called moderation in eating (bhojane mattaññutā). A person endowed with this moderation in eating is called 'one who is moderate in eating' (bhojane mattaññū).

Who is the person of established mindfulness (upaṭṭhitassati)? What is that mindfulness? That which is mindfulness, recollection, recall, mindfulness, the state of remembering, non-superficiality, non-forgetfulness, mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, right mindfulness—this is called mindfulness. A person endowed with this mindfulness is called 'one of established mindfulness' (upaṭṭhitassati).

Who is the person of clear comprehension (sampajāno)? What is that clear comprehension (sampajañña)? That which is wisdom, understanding, investigation, close investigation, investigation of phenomena, discernment, scrutiny, close scrutiny, erudition, skill, subtlety, clarity, thought, examination, breadth, sagacity, guidance, insight, clear comprehension, a goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the splendor of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called clear comprehension (sampajañña). A person endowed with this clear comprehension is called 'one of clear comprehension' (sampajāno).

Who is the person possessed of virtue (sīlasampanno)? What is that accomplishment in virtue (sīlasampadā)? Non-transgression by body, non-transgression by speech, non-transgression by both body and speech—this is called accomplishment in virtue (sīlasampadā). All restraint of virtue is also called accomplishment in virtue (sīlasampadā). A person endowed with this accomplishment in virtue is called 'one possessed of virtue' (sīlasampanno).

Who is the person possessed of view (diṭṭhisampanno)? What is that accomplishment in view (diṭṭhisampadā)? (There is the view that:) 'There is what is given, there is what is offered, there is what is sacrificed; there is the fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously born beings; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have fared rightly, who have practiced rightly, and who, having realized this world and the other world by their own direct knowledge, make them known.' Such wisdom, understanding... [as above] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called accomplishment in view (diṭṭhisampadā). All right view is also called accomplishment in view (diṭṭhisampadā). A person endowed with this accomplishment in view is called 'one possessed of view' (diṭṭhisampanno).

Which two persons are rare in the world? He who is first to do a favor (pubbakārī), and he who is grateful and appreciative (kataññū katavedī)—these two persons are rare in the world.
129:
Which two persons are difficult to satisfy (duttappayā)? He who hoards whatever he gets, and he who squanders (wastes) whatever he gets—these two persons are called those who are difficult to satisfy.

Which two persons are easy to satisfy (sutappayā)? He who does not hoard whatever he gets, and he who does not squander (waste) whatever he gets—these two persons are called those who are easy to satisfy.

In which two persons do the taints (āsavā) increase? He who feels remorse for what is not a matter for remorse, and he who does not feel remorse for what is a matter for remorse—in these two persons the taints increase.

In which two persons do the taints (āsavā) not increase? He who does not feel remorse for what is not a matter for remorse, and he who feels remorse for what is a matter for remorse—in these two persons the taints do not increase.

Who is the person of low inclination (hīnādhimutto)? Here, a certain person is immoral, of evil character; he associates with, frequents, and attends upon another who is immoral and of evil character—this person is called 'one of low inclination'.

Who is the person of superior inclination (paṇītādhimutto)? Here, a certain person is virtuous, of good character; he associates with, frequents, and attends upon another who is virtuous and of good character—this person is called 'one of superior inclination'.

Who is the satisfied person (titto)? The Paccekabuddhas and those disciples of the Blessed One who are Arahants are satisfied persons. The Perfectly Enlightened Buddha is both satisfied himself and one who satisfies others.

## Exposition of the Twos.

## 3. Designation of the Groups of Three

Who is the person without hope (nirāsa) [regarding the fruit of Arahantship]? Here, a certain person is immoral, of evil character, of impure and suspicious conduct, secretive in his actions...
130:
He who is not a recluse but claims to be a recluse, who is not a celibate but claims to be a celibate, who is corrupt within, leaking with lust, and like a heap of rubbish. He hears: "A certain bhikkhu, they say, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein." It does not occur to him: "When shall I too, through the destruction of the taints, realize for myself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwell therein?" This person is called "hopeless" (nirāsa).

And what kind of person is "hopeful" (āsaṃsa)? Here, a certain person is virtuous and of good character. He hears: "A certain bhikkhu, they say, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein." It occurs to him: "When shall I too, through the destruction of the taints, realize for myself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwell therein?" This person is called "hopeful" (āsaṃsa).

And what kind of person is "one whose hope has ceased" (vigatāsa)? Here, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. He hears: "A certain bhikkhu, they say, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein." It does not occur to him: "When shall I too, through the destruction of the taints, realize for myself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwell therein?" Why is that? Because the hope for liberation that he had previously when he was not yet liberated has now been stilled. This person is called "one whose hope has ceased" (vigatāsa).

In this regard, what are the three types of persons compared to a sick person (gilāna)? There are three types of sick persons: Here, a certain sick person, whether he obtains suitable food or not, whether he obtains suitable medicine or not, whether he obtains a suitable attendant or not, does not recover from that illness. (1)

Here, another sick person, whether he obtains suitable food or not, whether he obtains suitable...
131:
(2) ...medicine or not, whether he obtains a suitable attendant or not, he recovers from that illness.

(3) Here, another sick person recovers from that illness only if he obtains suitable food, not if he does not; only if he obtains suitable medicine, not if he does not; only if he obtains a suitable attendant, not if he does not.

Among these three types of sick persons, it is because of this sick person who recovers from illness only if he obtains suitable food, medicine, and an attendant that the Blessed One allowed food for the sick, medicine for the sick, and an attendant for the sick. And because of this sick person, other sick persons should also be attended to.

In the same way, there are three types of persons compared to a sick person existing in the world. What are the three?

(1) Here, a certain person, whether he gets to see the Tathāgata or not, whether he gets to hear the Dhamma-Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata or not, does not enter upon the fixed course of rightness (magga-niyāma) in wholesome states.

(2) Here, a certain person, whether he gets to see the Tathāgata or not, whether he gets to hear the Dhamma-Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata or not, enters upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.

(3) Here, a certain person enters upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states only if he gets to see the Tathāgata, not if he does not; only if he gets to hear the Dhamma-Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata, not if he does not.

Among these persons, [it is because of the person who enters the path] only if he gets to see the Tathāgata, not if he does not; only if he gets to hear the Dhamma-Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata, not if he does not
132:
It is not that [the Dhamma] should not be heard, but because of this person who is capable of entering the path of assurance (magga-niyāma) which is unswerving in wholesome states, the Blessed One has permitted the preaching of the Dhamma; and for the sake of this person, the Dhamma should also be preached to others. These are the three types of persons found existing in the world who are like the sick.

Who is the person who is a body-witness (kāyasakkhī)? Here, a certain person dwells having touched the eight liberations (vimokkha) with the mental body, and having seen with wisdom, some of his taints (āsava) are destroyed. This person is called a 'body-witness'.

Who is the person who has attained to view (diṭṭhippatta)? Here, a certain person understands 'This is suffering' as it really is; he understands 'This is the origin of suffering' as it really is; he understands 'This is the cessation of suffering' as it really is; he understands 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' as it really is. The teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata are also well seen and well practiced by him through wisdom. Having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are destroyed. This person is called 'one attained to view'.

Who is the person liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta)? Here, a certain person understands 'This is suffering' as it really is... [Pe]... The teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata are also well seen and well practiced by him through wisdom. Having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are destroyed. However, it is not in the same way as the one attained to view. This person is called 'one liberated by faith'.

Who is the person who speaks like dung (gūthabhāṇī)? Here, a certain person is a liar. When he is in an assembly, a congregation, among relatives, in a guild, or in the royal court, and is summoned and questioned as a witness—'Come, good man, tell what you know'—though he does not know, he says, 'I know'; or though he knows, he says, 'I do not know'; though he has not seen, he says, 'I have seen'; or though he has seen, he says, 'I have not seen.' Thus, for his own sake, for the sake of others, or for the sake of some small worldly gain, he consciously speaks lies. This person is called 'one who speaks like dung'.
133:
Who is the person who speaks like flowers (pupphabhāṇī)? Here, a certain person, having abandoned false speech, abstains from lying. When he is in an assembly, a congregation, among relatives, in a guild, or in the royal court, and is summoned and questioned as a witness—'Come, good man, tell what you know'—if he does not know, he says, 'I do not know'; if he knows, he says, 'I know'; if he has not seen, he says, 'I have not seen'; if he has seen, he says, 'I have seen.' Thus, for his own sake, for the sake of others, or for the sake of some small worldly gain, he does not consciously speak lies. This person is called 'one who speaks like flowers'.

Who is the person who speaks like honey (madhubhāṇī)? Here, a certain person is one who speaks such words as are blameless, pleasant to the ear, lovely, reaching the heart, polite, desired by many, and agreeable to many. This person is called 'one who speaks like honey'.

Who is the person with a mind like a sore (arukūpamacitto)? Here, a certain person is easily angered and much given to despair. Even when spoken to slightly, he becomes annoyed, angry, resentful, and stubborn; he displays anger, hatred, and discontent. Just as a festering sore, when struck by a stick or a shard, discharges even more matter, even so, here a certain person is easily angered and much given to despair. Even when spoken to slightly, he becomes annoyed, angry, resentful, and stubborn; he displays anger, hatred, and discontent. This person is called 'one with a mind like a sore'.

Who is the person with a mind like lightning (vijjūpamacitto)? Here, a certain person understands 'This is suffering' as it really is; he understands 'This is the origin of suffering' as it really is; he understands 'This is the cessation of suffering' as it really is; he understands 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' as it really is. Just as a man with sight might see objects in the dark of night during a flash of lightning, even so, here a certain person understands 'This is suffering' as it really is; he understands 'This is the origin of suffering' as it really is; he understands 'This is the cessation of suffering' as it really is...
134:
He understands as it really is: 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' This person is called 'one with a mind like lightning.'

And what kind of person is one with a mind like a diamond? Here, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself by direct knowledge in this very life. Just as there is nothing that a diamond cannot break, whether a gem or a stone, even so, here, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself by direct knowledge in this very life. This person is called 'one with a mind like a diamond.'

And what kind of person is the blind one? Here, a certain person does not have the kind of eye by which he might acquire wealth not yet acquired or increase wealth already acquired. He also does not have the kind of eye by which he might know wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, inferior and superior states, or states that are dark and bright opposites. This person is called 'the blind one.'

And what kind of person is the one-eyed? Here, a certain person has the kind of eye by which he might acquire wealth not yet acquired or increase wealth already acquired. However, he does not have the kind of eye by which he might know wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, inferior and superior states, or states that are dark and bright opposites. This person is called 'the one-eyed.'

And what kind of person is the two-eyed? Here, a certain person has the kind of eye by which he might acquire wealth not yet acquired or increase wealth already acquired. He also has the kind of eye by which he might know wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, inferior and superior states, or states that are dark and bright opposites. This person is called 'the two-eyed.'
135:
And what kind of person is one with upside-down wisdom? Here, a certain person frequently goes to the monastery to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the monks. The monks teach him the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and they proclaim the holy life that is entirely complete and pure. While sitting in that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that talk, does not attend to the middle, and does not attend to the end. Even after rising from that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that talk, does not attend to the middle, and does not attend to the end. Just as water poured into an overturned pot runs off and does not stay, even so, here, a certain person frequently goes to the monastery to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the monks. The monks teach him the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and they proclaim the holy life that is entirely complete and pure. While sitting in that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that talk, does not attend to the middle, and does not attend to the end. Even after rising from that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that talk, does not attend to the middle, and does not attend to the end. This person is called 'one with upside-down wisdom.'

And what kind of person is one with lap-like wisdom? Here, a certain person frequently goes to the monastery to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the monks. The monks teach him the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and they proclaim the holy life that is entirely complete and pure. While sitting in that seat, he attends to the beginning of that talk, attends to the middle, and attends to the end. However, after rising from that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that talk, does not attend to the middle, and does not attend to the end. Just as if a man had various kinds of foods—such as sesame, rice, cakes, and jujubes—heaped in his lap, and upon rising from that seat, he were to scatter them through lack of mindfulness; even so, here, a certain person frequently goes to the monastery to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the monks. The monks teach him the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle...
136:
...they proclaim the holy life that is good in the end, with meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure. That person, while sitting in that seat, attends to the beginning of that talk, attends to the middle, and attends to the end. But when he has risen from that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that talk, nor the middle, nor the end. This person is called "one of lap-like wisdom (ucchaṅgapañño)."

What kind of person is one of wide wisdom (puthupañño)? Here, a certain person goes frequently to the monastery to hear the Dhamma from the bhikkhus. The bhikkhus proclaim to him the holy life that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure. That person, while sitting in that seat, attends to the beginning of that talk, attends to the middle, and attends to the end. Even after rising from that seat, he attends to the beginning of that talk, attends to the middle, and attends to the end. Just as water poured into an upright jar stays there and does not flow out, even so, here a certain person goes frequently to the monastery to hear the Dhamma from the bhikkhus. The bhikkhus proclaim to him the holy life that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure. That person, while sitting in that seat, attends to the beginning of that talk, attends to the middle, and attends to the end. Even after rising from that seat, he attends to the beginning of that talk, attends to the middle, and attends to the end. This person is called "one of wide wisdom (puthupañño)."

What kind of person is not yet free from lust for sensual pleasures and for existence? The Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and the Once-returner (Sakadāgāmi). These persons are called "those not yet free from lust for sensual pleasures and for existence."

What kind of person is free from lust for sensual pleasures but not yet free from lust for existence? The Non-returner (Anāgāmī). This person is called "one who is free from lust for sensual pleasures but not yet free from lust for existence."

What kind of person is free from lust for sensual pleasures and for existence? The Arahant. This person is called "one who is free from lust for sensual pleasures and for existence."
137:
What kind of person is like an inscription on rock? Here, a certain person is frequently angry. And that anger of his persists for a long time. Just as an inscription on rock is not quickly destroyed by wind or water and lasts for a long time, even so, here a certain person is frequently angry, and that anger of his persists for a long time. This person is called "one like an inscription on rock."

What kind of person is like an inscription on earth? Here, a certain person is frequently angry. However, that anger of his does not persist for a long time. Just as an inscription on earth is quickly destroyed by wind or water and does not last for a long time, even so, here a certain person is frequently angry, but that anger of his does not persist for a long time. This person is called "one like an inscription on earth."

What kind of person is like an inscription on water? Here, a certain person, even when spoken to with very harsh words, rough words, or unpleasant words, remains friendly, companionable, and polite. Just as an inscription on water is quickly destroyed and does not last for a long time, even so, here a certain person, even when spoken to with very harsh, rough, or unpleasant words, remains friendly, companionable, and polite. This person is called "one like an inscription on water."

Among those, what are the three persons like hemp cloth (potthakūpama)? There are three kinds of hemp cloth: a new hemp cloth is of bad color, unpleasant to the touch, and of little value; a middle-aged hemp cloth is also of bad color, unpleasant to the touch, and of little value; an old hemp cloth is also of bad color, unpleasant to the touch, and of little value. An old hemp cloth is used for wiping soot from cooking pots or is thrown away on a rubbish heap. Even so, these three persons like hemp cloth are found among the bhikkhus. Which three? If a bhikkhu is new but is immoral and of bad character, this is his bad color. Just as that hemp cloth is of bad color...
138:
This person is like that (hempen cloth). For those who associate with, resort to, and follow the example of this person, it leads to their long-term harm and suffering. This is because of his unpleasant contact. Just as that hempen cloth is unpleasant to the touch, so too is this person. From whomsoever this person receives the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines for the sick, for them that offering is not of great fruit or great benefit. This is because of his low value. Just as that hempen cloth is of low value, so too is this person.

Whether he is a middle-aged monk ... (pe) ... or a senior monk, if he is immoral and of evil character, this is because of his bad appearance. Just as that hempen cloth is of bad appearance, so too is this person. For those who associate with, resort to, and follow the example of this person, it leads to their long-term harm and suffering. This is because of his unpleasant contact. Just as that hempen cloth is unpleasant to the touch, so too is this person. From whomsoever this person receives the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines for the sick, for them that offering is not of great fruit or great benefit. This is because of his low value. Just as that hempen cloth is of low value, so too is this person.

If such a senior monk speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha, the monks say to him: 'What is the use of the speech of an ignorant and unskilled person like you? Do you even think you should speak?' Being angry and displeased, he utters such words for which the Saṅgha expels him, just as one would throw that hempen cloth onto a rubbish heap. These are the three types of persons found among the monks who are like hempen cloth.

Among them, what are the three types of persons who are like Kāsian cloth? There are three types of Kāsian cloth: a new Kāsian cloth is beautiful in appearance, pleasant to the touch, and of great value. A middle-aged Kāsian cloth is also beautiful in appearance, pleasant to the touch, and of great value. An old Kāsian cloth is also beautiful in appearance, pleasant to the touch, and of great value. Even an old Kāsian cloth is used to wrap jewels or is kept in a perfume box.
139:
In the same way, these three types of persons who are like Kāsian cloth are found among the monks. What are the three?

If a new monk is virtuous and of good character, this is his beautiful appearance. Just as that Kāsian cloth is beautiful in appearance, so too is this person. For those who associate with, resort to, and follow the example of this monk, it leads to their long-term welfare and happiness. This is because of his pleasant contact. Just as that Kāsian cloth is pleasant to the touch, so too is this person. From whomsoever this monk receives the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines for the sick, for them that offering is of great fruit and great benefit. This is because of his great value. Just as that Kāsian cloth is of great value, so too is this person.

Whether he is a middle-aged monk ... (pe) ... or a senior monk, if he is virtuous and of good character, this is his beautiful appearance. Just as that Kāsian cloth is beautiful in appearance, so too is this person. For those who associate with, resort to, and follow the example of this monk, it leads to their long-term welfare and happiness. This is because of his pleasant contact. Just as that Kāsian cloth is pleasant to the touch, so too is this person. From whomsoever this monk receives the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines for the sick, for them that offering is of great fruit and great benefit. This is because of his great value. Just as that Kāsian cloth is of great value, so too is this person.

If such a senior monk speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha, the monks say: 'Venerables, be quiet; the senior monk is speaking Dhamma and Vinaya.' His words are worth treasuring in the mind, just like Kāsian cloth kept in a perfume box. These three types of persons are those found among the monks who are like Kāsian cloth.

And what person is easily measured? Here, a certain person is restless, haughty, frivolous, talkative, of loose speech, muddle-minded, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind and uncontrolled faculties. This person is called 'one who is easily measured'.

And what person is difficult to measure? Here, a certain person is not restless, not haughty, not frivolous, not talkative, not of loose speech ...
140:
A person who is endowed with established mindfulness, clear comprehension, a concentrated mind, a one-pointed mind, and restrained faculties—this person is called "one who is hard to measure (duppameyya)."

And what kind of person is immeasurable (appameyya)? In this world, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints (āsavas), enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself in this very life through direct knowledge. This person is called "immeasurable (appameyya)."

And what kind of person should not be associated with, followed, or attended upon? In this world, a certain person is inferior in virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā). Such a person should not be associated with, followed, or attended upon, except out of kindness and compassion.

And what kind of person should be associated with, followed, and attended upon? In this world, a certain person is one's equal in virtue, concentration, and wisdom. Such a person should be associated with, followed, and attended upon. For what reason? Thinking: "Since we are equal in virtue, there will be talk concerning virtue between us; that talk will be pleasant for us, and that talk will be continuous. Since we are equal in concentration, there will be talk concerning concentration between us; that talk will be pleasant for us, and that talk will be continuous. Since we are equal in wisdom, there will be talk concerning wisdom between us; that talk will be pleasant for us, and that talk will be continuous." Therefore, such a person should be associated with, followed, and attended upon.

And what kind of person should be associated with, followed, and attended upon with respect and honor? In this world, a certain person is superior to oneself in virtue, concentration, and wisdom. Such a person should be associated with, followed, and attended upon with respect and honor. For what reason? Thinking: "I shall fulfill the aggregate of virtue that is not yet fulfilled, or I shall support the fulfilled aggregate of virtue with wisdom in various ways. I shall fulfill the aggregate of concentration that is not yet fulfilled, or I shall support the fulfilled aggregate of concentration with wisdom in various ways. I shall fulfill the aggregate of wisdom that is not yet fulfilled, or I shall support the fulfilled aggregate of wisdom with wisdom in various ways." Therefore, such a person should be associated with, followed, and attended upon with respect and honor.
141:
And what kind of person is to be loathed, not associated with, not followed, and not attended upon? In this world, a certain person is immoral, of evil character, impure, of suspicious behavior, secretive in his actions, not a monk but claiming to be one, not a celibate but claiming to be one, rotten within, oozing with lust, and like a heap of rubbish. Such a person is to be loathed, not associated with, not followed, and not attended upon. For what reason? Even if one does not follow the example of such a person, a bad reputation spreads: "This person has evil friends, evil companions, and is inclined toward evil people." Just as a snake that has fallen into dung, even if it does not bite, smears one with filth; in the same way, even if one does not follow the example of such a person, a bad reputation spreads: "This person has evil friends, evil companions, and is inclined toward evil people." Therefore, such a person is to be loathed, not associated with, not followed, and not attended upon.

And what kind of person is to be treated with equanimity (ignored), not associated with, not followed, and not attended upon? In this world, a certain person is angry and full of despair; even when spoken to slightly, he becomes annoyed, angry, hostile, and resentful, manifesting anger, hatred, and discontent. Just as a festering sore, when struck by a stick or a shard, oozes even more matter; in the same way, a certain person is angry and full of despair... manifesting anger, hatred, and discontent. Just as an ember of tinduka wood, when struck by a stick or a shard, crackles and sputters even more; in the same way, a certain person is angry and full of despair... manifesting anger, hatred, and discontent. Just as a cesspool, when stirred with a stick or a shard, becomes even more foul-smelling; in the same way, a certain person in this world is angry and full of despair; even when spoken to slightly, he becomes annoyed, angry, hostile, and resentful, manifesting anger, hatred, and discontent. Such a person is to be treated with equanimity, not associated with, not followed, and not attended upon. For what reason? Thinking: "He might abuse me, he might threaten me..."
142:
"He might even do me harm"—thinking thus, such a person should be looked upon with indifference; he should not be associated with, not frequented, and not attended upon. What kind of person should be associated with, frequented, and attended upon? Here, a certain person is virtuous and of good character. Such a person should be associated with, frequented, and attended upon. What is the reason for this? Even if one does not follow the views of such a person, a good reputation spreads about him: "This man is one who has good friends, good companions, and is inclined towards the good." Therefore, such a person should be associated with, frequented, and attended upon.

What kind of person is one who fulfills virtue, but practices concentration and wisdom only to a moderate extent? The Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and the Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī). These persons are called those who fulfill virtue, but practice concentration and wisdom only to a moderate extent.

What kind of person is one who fulfills virtue and concentration, but practices wisdom only to a moderate extent? The Non-returner (Anāgāmī). This person is called one who fulfills virtue and concentration, but practices wisdom only to a moderate extent.

What kind of person is one who fulfills virtue, concentration, and wisdom? The Arahant. This person is called one who fulfills virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

In that context, who are the three teachers? Here, a certain teacher describes the full understanding of sensual desires, but does not describe the full understanding of forms, nor the full understanding of feelings. Here, another teacher describes the full understanding of sensual desires and the full understanding of forms, but does not describe the full understanding of feelings. Here, another teacher describes the full understanding of sensual desires, the full understanding of forms, and the full understanding of feelings.

Among those teachers, the teacher who describes the full understanding of sensual desires but not of forms or feelings should be known as a teacher who has attained the meditative attainments of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-samāpatti). Among those teachers, the teacher who describes the full understanding of sensual desires...
143:
...and describes the full understanding of forms, but does not describe the full understanding of feelings, should be known as a teacher who has attained the meditative attainments of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara-samāpatti). Among those teachers, the teacher who describes the full understanding of sensual desires, the full understanding of forms, and the full understanding of feelings should be known as the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha). These are the three teachers.

In that context, who are the other three teachers? Here, a certain teacher describes the self as real and permanent in the present life, and also describes the self as real and permanent in the future life. Here, another teacher describes the self as real and permanent in the present life, but does not describe the self as real and permanent in the future life. Here, another teacher does not describe the self as real and permanent in the present life, nor does he describe the self as real and permanent in the future life.

Among those teachers, the teacher who describes the self as real and permanent in the present life and also in the future life should be known as a teacher who holds the eternalist view (sassatavāda). Among those teachers, the teacher who describes the self as real and permanent in the present life but not in the future life should be known as a teacher who holds the annihilationist view (ucchedavāda). Among those teachers, the teacher who does not describe the self as real and permanent in the present life nor in the future life should be known as the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha). These are the other three teachers.

## Exposition of the Groups of Three (Tikaniddesa).

## 4. Designation of Individuals by Groups of Four (Catukka-puggalapaññatti)

What kind of person is an unworthy person (asappurisa)? Here, a certain person kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehoods, and indulges in fermented and distilled liquors which cause heedlessness. This person is called an "unworthy person."

What kind of person is more unworthy than an unworthy person? Here, a certain person kills living beings himself and [encourages] others in killing living beings...
144: ...encourages others to do so. He himself takes what is not given and encourages others to take what is not given. He himself engages in sexual misconduct and encourages others to engage in sexual misconduct. He himself speaks falsehood and encourages others to speak falsehood. He himself indulges in fermented and distilled liquors, which are the basis for negligence, and encourages others to indulge in fermented and distilled liquors. This person is called 'one who is worse than a bad person'. What kind of person is a good person (sappurisa)? Here, a certain person abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from fermented and distilled liquors, which are the basis for negligence. This person is called 'a good person'. What kind of person is one who is better than a good person? Here, a certain person himself abstains from killing living beings and encourages others to abstain from killing living beings. He himself abstains from taking what is not given and encourages others to abstain from taking what is not given. He himself abstains from sexual misconduct and encourages others to abstain from sexual misconduct. He himself abstains from false speech and encourages others to abstain from false speech. He himself abstains from fermented and distilled liquors, which are the basis for negligence, and encourages others to abstain from fermented and distilled liquors. This person is called 'one who is better than a good person'. What kind of person is an evil person (pāpa)? Here, a certain person is one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisive speech, speaks harsh speech, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, has a mind of ill will, and holds wrong view. This person is called 'an evil person'. What kind of person is one who is worse than an evil person? Here, a certain person himself kills living beings and encourages others to kill living beings,
145: He himself takes what is not given and encourages others to take what is not given. He himself engages in sexual misconduct and encourages others to engage in sexual misconduct. He himself speaks falsehood and encourages others to speak falsehood. He himself speaks divisive speech and encourages others to speak divisive speech. He himself speaks harsh speech and encourages others to speak harsh speech. He himself engages in idle chatter and encourages others to engage in idle chatter. He himself is covetous and encourages others to be covetous. He himself has a mind of ill will and encourages others to have ill will. He himself holds wrong view and encourages others to hold wrong view. This person is called 'one who is worse than an evil person'. What kind of person is a virtuous person (kalyāṇa)? Here, a certain person is one who abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, abstains from divisive speech, abstains from harsh speech, abstains from idle chatter, is not covetous, has no ill will, and holds right view. This person is called 'a virtuous person'. What kind of person is one who is better than a virtuous person? Here, a certain person himself abstains from killing living beings and encourages others to abstain from killing living beings. He himself abstains from taking what is not given and encourages others to abstain from taking what is not given. He himself abstains from sexual misconduct and encourages others to abstain from sexual misconduct. He himself abstains from false speech and encourages others to abstain from false speech. He himself abstains from divisive speech and encourages others to abstain from divisive speech. He himself abstains from harsh speech and encourages others to abstain from harsh speech. He himself abstains from idle chatter and encourages others to abstain from idle chatter. He himself is not covetous and encourages others to be not covetous. He himself has no ill will and encourages others to have no ill will. He himself holds right view
146:
He also encourages others in Right View. This person is called "one who is better than the good."

What kind of person is of evil nature? Here, a certain person is one who kills living beings, takes what is not given... (pe) ... holds wrong views. This person is called "one of evil nature."

What kind of person is more evil than one of evil nature? Here, a certain person himself kills living beings and encourages others to kill living beings; himself takes what is not given and encourages others to take what is not given... (pe) ... himself holds wrong views and encourages others to hold wrong views. This person is called "one who is more evil than one of evil nature."

What kind of person is of good nature? Here, a certain person abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given... (pe) ... holds right views. This person is called "one of good nature."

What kind of person is better than one of good nature? Here, a certain person himself abstains from killing living beings and encourages others to abstain from killing living beings... (pe) ... himself holds right views and encourages others to hold right views. This person is called "one who is better than one of good nature."

What kind of person is blameworthy? Here, a certain person is possessed of blameworthy bodily action, blameworthy verbal action, and blameworthy mental action. This person is called "blameworthy."

What kind of person is mostly blameworthy?
