Here, a certain person is possessed of much blameworthy bodily action and little blameless bodily action; much blameworthy verbal action and little blameless verbal action; much blameworthy mental action and little blameless mental action. This person is called "mostly blameworthy."
147:
What kind of person is one of few faults (appavajjo)? Here, a certain person is possessed of much blameless bodily action and little blameworthy bodily action; much blameless verbal action and little blameworthy verbal action; much blameless mental action and little blameworthy mental action. This person is called "one of few faults" (appavajjo).

What kind of person is blameless (anavajjo)? Here, a certain person is possessed of blameless bodily action, blameless verbal action, and blameless mental action. This person is called "blameless" (anavajjo).

What kind of person is one who understands through brief instruction (ugghaṭitaññū)? For a certain person, the penetration of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) occurs simultaneously with the time the Dhamma is declared. This person is called "one who understands through brief instruction" (ugghaṭitaññū).

What kind of person is one who understands through detailed explanation (vipañcitaññū)? For a certain person, the penetration of the Dhamma occurs when the meaning of what was spoken in brief is being analyzed in detail. This person is called "one who understands through detailed explanation" (vipañcitaññū).

What kind of person is one who needs guidance (neyyo)? For a certain person, the penetration of the Dhamma occurs gradually through recitation, through repeated questioning, through wise attention, and through associating with, following, and attending upon good friends (kalyāṇamitta). This person is called "one who needs guidance" (neyyo).

What kind of person is one for whom the word is the maximum (padaparamo)? For a certain person, although he hears much, speaks much, memorizes much, and teaches much, the penetration of the Dhamma does not occur in that lifetime. This person is called "one for whom the word is the maximum" (padaparamo).

What kind of person is one who has relevant wit but not quick wit (yuttappaṭibhāno no muttappaṭibhāno)? Here, a certain person, when asked a question, can give a relevant answer but not quickly. This person is called "one who has relevant wit but not quick wit" (yuttappaṭibhāno no muttappaṭibhāno).
148:
What kind of person is one who has ready wit but not reasoned wit? Here, a certain person, when asked a question, can answer quickly but cannot provide an answer that is logical and reasoned. This person is called "one who has ready wit but not reasoned wit."

What kind of person is one who has both reasoned wit and ready wit? Here, a certain person, when asked a question, can answer both logically and quickly. This person is called "one who has both reasoned wit and ready wit."

What kind of person is one who has neither reasoned wit nor ready wit? Here, a certain person, when asked a question, can answer neither logically nor quickly. This person is called "one who has neither reasoned wit nor ready wit."

Among them, who are the four types of persons who are Dhamma preachers? Here, a certain Dhamma preacher speaks little of the Dhamma and speaks what is not meaningful (unconnected to the goal), and his audience is also not skilled in distinguishing what is meaningful from what is not. Such a Dhamma preacher is known as a "Dhamma preacher" only to such an audience.

Here, a certain Dhamma preacher speaks little of the Dhamma but speaks what is meaningful, and his audience is skilled in distinguishing what is meaningful from what is not. Such a Dhamma preacher is known as a "Dhamma preacher" only to such an audience.

Here, a certain Dhamma preacher speaks much of the Dhamma but speaks what is not meaningful, and his audience is not skilled in distinguishing what is meaningful from what is not. Such a Dhamma preacher is known as a "Dhamma preacher" only to such an audience.

Here, a certain Dhamma preacher speaks much of the Dhamma and also speaks what is meaningful, and his audience is skilled in distinguishing what is meaningful from what is not. Such a Dhamma preacher is known as a "Dhamma preacher" only to such an audience. These are the four types of "Dhamma preachers."

Among them, who are the four types of persons compared to clouds? There are four types of clouds: those that thunder but do not rain, those that rain but do not thunder, those that both thunder and rain, and those that neither thunder nor rain. Even so, these four types of persons compared to clouds are found existing in the world. Which four?
149:
Which four? Those that thunder but do not rain, those that rain but do not thunder, those that both thunder and rain, and those that neither thunder nor rain.

How is a person like a cloud that thunders but does not rain? Here, a certain person is a talker but not a doer. Thus, a person is like a cloud that thunders but does not rain. Just as that cloud thunders but does not rain, so too is this person.

How is a person like a cloud that rains but does not thunder? Here, a certain person is a doer but not a talker. Thus, a person is like a cloud that rains but does not thunder. Just as that cloud rains but does not thunder, so too is this person.

How is a person like a cloud that both thunders and rains? Here, a certain person is both a talker and a doer. Thus, a person is like a cloud that both thunders and rains. Just as that cloud both thunders and rains, so too is this person.

How is a person like a cloud that neither thunders nor rains? Here, a certain person is neither a talker nor a doer. Thus, a person is like a cloud that neither thunders nor rains. Just as that cloud neither thunders nor rains, so too is this person.

These four types of persons compared to clouds are found existing in the world.

In that regard, who are the four types of persons compared to mice? There are four types of mice: those that dig a hole but do not live in it, those that live in a hole but do not dig it, those that both dig and live in it, and those that neither dig nor live in it. Even so, these four types of persons compared to mice are found existing in the world. Which four? Those that dig but do not live, those that live but do not dig, those that both dig and live, and those that neither dig nor live.

How is a person like a mouse that digs a hole but does not live in it? Here, a certain person learns the Dhamma—the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. Yet, he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"; he does not understand as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; he does not understand as it really is: "This is...
150:
...'This is the cessation of suffering,' he does not truly know it as it really is; 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,' he does not truly know it as it really is. In this way, the person is like a mouse that only digs a hole but does not live in it. For example, just as that mouse only digs a hole but does not live in it, this person is just like that mouse.

How is a person like a mouse that only lives in a hole but does not dig it? In this world, a certain person does not learn the Pariyatti Dhamma—the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. However, that person truly knows 'This is suffering' as it really is; he truly knows 'This is the origin of suffering' as it really is; he truly knows 'This is the cessation of suffering' as it really is; and he truly knows 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' as it really is. In this way, the person is like a mouse that only lives in a hole but does not dig it. For example, just as that mouse only lives in a hole but does not dig it, this person is just like that mouse.

How is a person like a mouse that both digs a hole and lives in it? In this world, a certain person learns the Pariyatti Dhamma—the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. That person truly knows 'This is suffering' as it really is; he truly knows 'This is the origin of suffering' as it really is; he truly knows 'This is the cessation of suffering' as it really is; and he truly knows 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' as it really is. In this way, the person is like a mouse that both digs a hole and lives in it. For example, just as that mouse both digs a hole and lives in it, this person is just like that mouse.

How is a person like a mouse that neither digs a hole nor lives in it? In this world, a certain person does not learn the Pariyatti Dhamma—the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. That person does not truly know 'This is suffering' as it really is; he does not truly know 'This is the origin of suffering' as it really is; he does not truly know 'This is the cessation of suffering' as it really is; and he does not truly know 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' as it really is. In this way, the person is like a mouse that neither digs a hole nor lives in it. For example, just as that mouse neither digs a hole nor lives in it, this person is just like that mouse.

These four types of persons, similar to mice, exist in the world.
151:
Among those [four types of persons], what are the four types of persons similar to mangoes? There are four types of mangoes: those that are unripe but have the appearance of being ripe, those that are ripe but have the appearance of being unripe, those that are unripe and have the appearance of being unripe, and those that are ripe and have the appearance of being ripe. In the same way, these four types of persons similar to mangoes exist in the world. What are the four? The person who is unripe but has the appearance of being ripe, the person who is ripe but has the appearance of being unripe, the person who is unripe and has the appearance of being unripe, and the person who is ripe and has the appearance of being ripe.

How is a person unripe but having the appearance of being ripe? In this Dispensation, a certain person's going forward, returning, looking ahead, looking aside, bending, stretching, and wearing of the inner robe, double robe, and carrying of the bowl and robes are inspiring. However, that person does not truly know 'This is suffering' as it really is; he does not truly know 'This is the origin of suffering' as it really is; he does not truly know 'This is the cessation of suffering' as it really is; and he does not truly know 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' as it really is. In this way, the person is unripe but has the appearance of being ripe. Just as that mango which is unripe but has the appearance of being ripe is such, this person is just like that mango.

How is a person ripe but having the appearance of being unripe? In this Dispensation, a certain person's going forward, returning, looking ahead, looking aside, bending, stretching, and wearing of the inner robe, double robe, and carrying of the bowl and robes are not inspiring. However, that person truly knows 'This is suffering' as it really is; he truly knows 'This is the origin of suffering' as it really is; he truly knows 'This is the cessation of suffering' as it really is; and he truly knows 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' as it really is. In this way, the person is ripe but has the appearance of being unripe. Just as that mango which is ripe but has the appearance of being unripe is such, this person is just like that mango.

How is a person unripe and having the appearance of being unripe? In this Dispensation, a certain person's going forward, returning, looking ahead, looking aside, bending, stretching, and wearing of the inner robe, double robe, and carrying of the bowl and robes are not inspiring. That person does not truly know 'This is suffering' as it really is... [and so on]... he does not truly know 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' as it really is. In this way, the person is unripe and has the appearance of being unripe. Just as that mango which is unripe and has the appearance of being unripe is such, this person is just like that mango.

How is a person ripe and having the appearance of being ripe? In this Dispensation, a certain person's going forward, returning, looking ahead, looking aside, bending, stretching, and wearing of the inner robe, double robe, and carrying of the bowl and robes are inspiring. That person truly knows 'This is suffering' as it really is...
152:
...knows... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' as it really is. In this way, the person is ripe and has the appearance of being ripe. Just as that mango is ripe and has the appearance of being ripe, so too is this person.
These are the four types of persons similar to mangoes found existing in the world.

Among those, what are the four types of persons similar to pots? There are four types of pots: empty and closed, full and open, empty and open, and full and closed. In the same way, these four types of persons similar to pots are found existing in the world. What are the four? The empty and closed, the full and open, the empty and open, and the full and closed.

And how is a person empty and closed? Here, a certain person's moving forward and returning, looking ahead and looking away, bending and stretching, and wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes are graceful. But he does not know as it really is: 'This is suffering'... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' In this way, the person is empty and closed. Just as that pot is empty and closed, so too is this person.

And how is a person full and open? Here, a certain person's moving forward and returning, looking ahead and looking away, bending and stretching, and wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes are not graceful. But he knows as it really is: 'This is suffering'... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' In this way, the person is full and open. Just as that pot is full and open, so too is this person.

And how is a person empty and open? Here, a certain person's moving forward and returning, looking ahead and looking away, bending and stretching, and wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes are not graceful. And he does not know as it really is: 'This is suffering'... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' In this way, the person is empty and open. Just as that pot is empty and open, so too is this person.

And how is a person full and closed? Here, a certain person's moving forward and returning, looking ahead and looking away, bending and stretching, and wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes are graceful.
153:
...bending and stretching, and wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes (are graceful). He knows as it really is: 'This is suffering'... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' In this way, the person is full (of Dhamma) and closed (in faculties). Just as that pot is full and closed, so too is this person. These four types of persons similar to pots are found existing in the world.

Among those, what are the four types of persons similar to water pools? There are four types of water pools: shallow but appearing deep, deep but appearing shallow, shallow and appearing shallow, and deep and appearing deep. In the same way, these four types of persons similar to water pools are found existing in the world. What are the four? The one who is shallow but appears deep, the one who is deep but appears shallow, the one who is shallow and appears shallow, and the one who is deep and appears deep.

And how is a person shallow but appearing deep? Here, a certain person's moving forward and returning, looking ahead and looking away, bending and stretching, and wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes are graceful. But he does not know as it really is: 'This is suffering'... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' In this way, the person is shallow but appearing deep. Just as that water pool is shallow but appearing deep, so too is this person.

And how is a person deep but appearing shallow? Here, a certain person's moving forward and returning, looking ahead and looking away, bending and stretching, and wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes are not graceful. But he knows as it really is: 'This is suffering'... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' In this way, the person is deep but appearing shallow. Just as that water pool is deep but appearing shallow, so too is this person.

And how is a person shallow and appearing shallow? Here, a certain person's moving forward and returning, looking ahead and looking away, bending and stretching, and wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes are not graceful. And he does not know as it really is: 'This is suffering'... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' as...
154:
...does not know as it really is. In this way, the person is shallow and appears shallow. Just as that pool of water is shallow and appears shallow, this person is like that pool of water.

How is a person deep and appears deep? In this world, a certain person's advancing, retreating, looking straight ahead, looking aside, bending, stretching, and wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes are inspiring. He knows as it really is: "This is suffering"... He knows as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, the person is deep and appears deep. Just as that pool of water is deep and appears deep, this person is like that pool of water. These four types of persons compared to pools of water are found existing in the world.

Among those four, what are the four types of persons compared to bulls? There are four types of bulls: a bull that is fierce in its own herd but not in another's herd; a bull that is fierce in another's herd but not in its own herd; a bull that is fierce in its own herd and also in another's herd; and a bull that is fierce neither in its own herd nor in another's herd. In the same way, these four types of persons compared to bulls are found existing in the world. What are the four? One who is fierce in his own assembly but not in another's assembly; one who is fierce in another's assembly but not in his own assembly; one who is fierce in his own assembly and also in another's assembly; and one who is fierce neither in his own assembly nor in another's assembly.

How is a person fierce in his own assembly but not in another's assembly? In this world, a certain person is one who terrifies his own assembly, but not another's assembly. In this way, the person is fierce in his own assembly but not in another's assembly. Just as that bull is fierce in its own herd but not in another's herd, this person is like that bull.

How is a person fierce in another's assembly but not in his own assembly? In this world, a certain person is one who terrifies another's assembly, but not his own assembly. In this way, the person is fierce in another's assembly but not in his own assembly. Just as that bull is fierce in another's herd but not in its own herd, this person is like that bull.

How is a person fierce in his own assembly and also in another's assembly? In this world, a certain person is one who terrifies his own assembly and also another's assembly. In this way...
155:
...the person is fierce in his own herd and also in another's herd. Just as that bull is fierce in its own herd and also in another's herd, this person is like that bull.

How is a person fierce neither in his own herd nor in another's herd? In this world, a certain person is one who terrifies neither his own assembly nor another's assembly. In this way, the person is fierce neither in his own herd nor in another's herd. Just as that bull is fierce neither in its own herd nor in another's herd, this person is like that bull. These four types of persons compared to snakes are found existing in the world.

Among those, what are the four types of persons compared to venomous snakes? There are four types of venomous snakes: a snake whose venom is quick-acting but not intense; a snake whose venom is intense but not quick-acting; a snake whose venom is both quick-acting and intense; and a snake whose venom is neither quick-acting nor intense. In the same way, these four types of persons compared to venomous snakes are found existing in the world. What are the four? One whose venom is quick-acting but not intense; one whose venom is intense but not quick-acting; one whose venom is both quick-acting and intense; and one whose venom is neither quick-acting nor intense.

How is a person one whose venom is quick-acting but not intense? In this world, a certain person frequently gets angry. However, that anger of his does not persist for a long time, for a long night. In this way, the person is one whose venom is quick-acting but not intense. Just like that snake whose venom is quick-acting but not intense, this person is like that snake.

How is a person one whose venom is intense but not quick-acting? In this world, a certain person does not frequently get angry. However, that anger of his persists for a long time, for a long night. In this way, the person is one whose venom is intense but not quick-acting. Just like that snake whose venom is intense but not quick-acting, this person is like that snake.

How is a person one whose venom is both quick-acting and intense? In this world, a certain person frequently gets angry. That anger of his also persists for a long time, for a long night. In this way, the person is one whose venom is both quick-acting and intense.
156:
Just like that snake whose venom is both spreading and fierce, this person is similar to that snake.

How is a person one whose venom is neither spreading nor fierce? Here, a certain person does not get angry often. And that anger of his does not persist for a long time, for a long night. In this way, a person is one whose venom is neither spreading nor fierce. Just like that snake whose venom is neither spreading nor fierce, this person is similar to that snake. These four types of persons similar to snakes are found existing in the world.

How does a person, without investigating and without scrutinizing, and without probing into their qualities, speak the praise of one who does not deserve praise? Here, a certain person speaks the praise of those of other sects (titthiyas) and disciples of other sects who have practiced wrongly and have practiced incorrectly, saying: "They have practiced well," or "They have practiced rightly." In this way, a person, without investigating and without scrutinizing, and without probing into their qualities, speaks the praise of one who does not deserve praise.

How does a person, without investigating and without scrutinizing, and without probing into their qualities, speak the dispraise of one who deserves praise? Here, a certain person speaks the dispraise of the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas who have practiced well and have practiced rightly, saying: "They have practiced wrongly," or "They have practiced incorrectly." In this way, a person, without investigating and without scrutinizing, and without probing into their qualities, speaks the dispraise of one who deserves praise.

How does a person, without investigating and without scrutinizing, and without probing into their qualities, manifest confidence in a matter that is not inspiring? Here, a certain person engenders confidence in a wrong practice or an incorrect practice, saying: "It is a good practice," or "It is a right practice." In this way, a person, without investigating and without scrutinizing, and without probing into their qualities, manifests confidence in a matter that is not inspiring.

How does a person, without investigating and without scrutinizing, and without probing into their qualities, manifest a lack of confidence in a matter that is inspiring? Here, a certain person engenders a lack of confidence in a good practice or a right practice, saying: "It is a wrong practice," or "It is an incorrect practice." In this way, a person, without investigating and without scrutinizing, and without probing into their qualities, manifests a lack of confidence in a matter that is inspiring.
157:
How does a person, having investigated and having scrutinized, and having probed into their qualities, speak the dispraise of one who deserves dispraise? Here, a certain person speaks the dispraise of those of other sects (titthiyas) and disciples of other sects who have practiced wrongly and have practiced incorrectly, saying: 'They have practiced wrongly,' or 'They have practiced incorrectly.' In this way, a person, having investigated and having scrutinized, and having probed into their qualities, speaks the dispraise of one who deserves dispraise.

How does a person, having investigated and having scrutinized, and having probed into their qualities, speak the praise of one who deserves praise? Here, a certain person speaks the praise of the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas who have practiced well and have practiced correctly and rightly, saying: 'They have practiced well,' or 'They have practiced correctly and rightly.' In this way, a person, having investigated and having scrutinized, and having probed into their qualities, speaks the praise of one who deserves praise.

How does a person, having investigated and having scrutinized, and having probed into their qualities, manifest a lack of confidence in a matter that is not inspiring? Here, a certain person engenders a lack of confidence in a wrong practice or an incorrect practice, saying: 'It is a wrong practice,' or 'It is an incorrect practice.' In this way, a person, having investigated and having scrutinized, and having probed into their qualities, manifests a lack of confidence in a matter that is not inspiring.

How does a person, having investigated and having scrutinized, and having probed into their qualities, manifest confidence in a matter that is inspiring? Here, a certain person engenders confidence in a good practice or an unerring and right practice, saying: 'It is a good practice,' or 'It is an unerring and right practice.' In this way, a person, having investigated and having scrutinized, and having probed into their qualities, manifests confidence in a matter that is inspiring.

How is a person one who speaks the dispraise of one who deserves dispraise—truthfully, factually, and at the right time—but does not speak the praise of one who deserves praise—truthfully, factually, and at the right time? Here, a certain person has both virtues and faults. Whatever fault exists in that person, he speaks of that fault truthfully, factually, and at the right time. But whatever virtue exists in that person, he does not speak of that virtue truthfully, factually, and at the right time. In this way, a person is one who speaks the dispraise of one who deserves dispraise—truthfully, factually, and at the right time—but does not speak the praise of one who deserves praise—truthfully, factually, and at the right time.

How is a person one who speaks the praise of one who deserves praise—truthfully, factually, and at the right time—but does not speak the dispraise of one who deserves dispraise—truthfully, factually, and at the right time? Here, a certain person has both virtues and faults ...
158:
There is. Among them, if there is a praiseworthy quality, he speaks of that quality according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time. If there is a blameworthy fault, he does not speak of that fault according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time. Thus, the person is one who speaks praise of the praiseworthy according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time, but is not one who speaks blame of the blameworthy according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time.

And how is a person one who speaks blame of the blameworthy according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time, and also speaks praise of the praiseworthy according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time? In this world, a certain person has both praiseworthy qualities and blameworthy faults. Among them, if there is a blameworthy fault, he speaks of that fault according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time. If there is a praiseworthy quality, he also speaks of that quality according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time. In that matter, he is one who knows the proper time to answer that question. Thus, the person is one who speaks blame of the blameworthy according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time, and also speaks praise of the praiseworthy according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time.

And how is a person one who neither speaks blame of the blameworthy according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time, nor speaks praise of the praiseworthy according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time? In this world, a certain person has both praiseworthy qualities and blameworthy faults. Among them, even if there is a blameworthy fault, he does not speak of that fault according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time. Even if there is a praiseworthy quality, he does not speak of that quality according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time. He dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Thus, the person is one who neither speaks blame of the blameworthy according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time, nor speaks praise of the praiseworthy according to the truth, correctly, and at the proper time.

Who is the person who lives by the fruit of effort, but not by the fruit of merit? For whichever person livelihood is achieved through rising up, striving, and making an effort, but not through merit—this person is called "one who lives by the fruit of effort, but not by the fruit of merit."

Who is the person who lives by the fruit of merit, but not by the fruit of effort? Starting from the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas, the devas above them live by the fruit of merit, not by the fruit of effort.
159:
Who is the person who lives by both the fruit of effort and the fruit of merit? For whichever person livelihood is achieved through rising up, striving, and making an effort, and also through merit—this person is called "one who lives by both the fruit of effort and the fruit of merit."

Who is the person who lives by neither the fruit of effort nor the fruit of merit? Beings reborn in hell live by neither the fruit of effort nor the fruit of merit.

And how is a person one who is in darkness and bound for darkness? In this world, a certain person is reborn in a low family—a family of Caṇḍālas, hunters, bamboo-weavers, chariot-makers, or sweepers. He is born into a family that is poor, with little food and drink, where livelihood is difficult, and where food and clothing are obtained with hardship. He is also ugly, unsightly, dwarfish, and full of diseases. He may be blind, crooked-handed, lame, or paralyzed. He does not regularly obtain food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, bedding, housing, and lighting. He performs misconduct by body, speech, and mind. Having performed misconduct by body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the nether world, hell. Thus, the person is one who is in darkness and bound for darkness.

And how is a person one who is in darkness and bound for light? In this world, a certain person is reborn in a low family—a family of Caṇḍālas, hunters, bamboo-weavers, chariot-makers, or sweepers. He is born into a family that is poor, with little food and drink, where livelihood is difficult, and where food and clothing are obtained with hardship. He is also ugly, unsightly, dwarfish, and full of diseases. He may be blind, crooked-handed, lame, or paralyzed. He does not regularly obtain food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, bedding, housing, and lighting. He performs good conduct by body, speech, and mind. Having performed good conduct by body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, the person is one who is in darkness and bound for light.

And how is a person one who is in light and bound for darkness? In this world, a certain person is reborn in a high family—such as a family of Khattiya-mahāsālas or...
160:
...or he is born into a wealthy Brāhmaṇa family, or a wealthy householder family, rich, with great wealth, great possessions, abundant gold and silver, abundant assets, and abundant property and grain. He is handsome, attractive, pleasing, and possessed of supreme beauty of complexion. He is a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, bedding, dwellings, and lighting. He practices misconduct by body, speech, and mind. Having practiced misconduct by body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a plane of misery, a bad destination, a lower world, in hell. Thus, the person is one who is light but bound for darkness.

And how is a person light and bound for light? Here, a certain person is born into a high family, that is, a wealthy Khattiya family, or a wealthy Brāhmaṇa family, or a wealthy householder family, rich, with great wealth, great possessions, abundant gold and silver, abundant assets, and abundant property and grain. He is handsome, attractive, pleasing, and possessed of supreme beauty of complexion. He is a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, bedding, dwellings, and lighting. He practices good conduct by body, speech, and mind. Having practiced good conduct by body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. Thus, the person is one who is light and bound for light.

And how is a person one who is low in this life and bound for lowness in the next? ... [pe] ... Thus, the person is one who is low in this life and bound for lowness in the next.

And how is a person one who is low in this life and bound for highness in the next? ... [pe] ... Thus, the person is one who is low in this life and bound for highness in the next.

And how is a person one who is high in this life and bound for lowness in the next? ... [pe] ... Thus, the person is one who is high in this life and bound for lowness in the next.

And how is a person one who is high in this life and bound for highness in the next? ... [pe] ... Thus, the person is one who is high in this life and bound for highness in the next.
161:
In that exposition, who are the four persons compared to trees? There are four kinds of trees: a tree that is sapwood surrounded by heartwood, a tree that is heartwood surrounded by sapwood, a tree that is sapwood surrounded by sapwood, and a tree that is heartwood surrounded by heartwood. In the same way, these four persons compared to trees are found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is sapwood surrounded by heartwood, the person who is heartwood surrounded by sapwood, the person who is sapwood surrounded by sapwood, and the person who is heartwood surrounded by heartwood.

And how is a person sapwood surrounded by heartwood? Here, a certain person is immoral and of evil nature, but his retinue is virtuous and of good nature. Thus, the person is sapwood surrounded by heartwood. Just as that tree is sapwood surrounded by heartwood, so too is this person.

And how is a person heartwood surrounded by sapwood? Here, a certain person is virtuous and of good nature, but his retinue is immoral and of evil nature. Thus, the person is heartwood surrounded by sapwood. Just as that tree is heartwood surrounded by sapwood, so too is this person.

And how is a person sapwood surrounded by sapwood? Here, a certain person is immoral and of evil nature, and his retinue is also immoral and of evil nature. Thus, the person is sapwood surrounded by sapwood. Just as that tree is sapwood surrounded by sapwood, so too is this person.

And how is a person heartwood surrounded by heartwood? Here, a certain person is virtuous and of good nature, and his retinue is also virtuous and of good nature. Thus, the person is heartwood surrounded by heartwood. Just as that tree is heartwood surrounded by heartwood, so too is this person. These four persons compared to trees are found existing in the world.

And what kind of person is one who measures by form and is confident in form? Here, a certain person, having seen height, or having seen girth, or having seen shape, or having seen perfection, takes a measure there and gains confidence. This person is called one who measures by form and is confident in form.
162:
What kind of person is one who measures by sound and is pleased by sound? Here, a certain person, taking as a measure the praise of others in their absence, the praise of others through compositions, the praise of others in their presence, or the carrying of others' reputations, generates confidence. This person is called one who measures by sound and is pleased by sound.

What kind of person is one who measures by austerity and is pleased by austerity? Here, a certain person, seeing the roughness of robes, or seeing the roughness of a bowl, or seeing the roughness of a lodging, or seeing various difficult practices, taking that as a measure, generates confidence. This person is called one who measures by austerity and is pleased by austerity.

What kind of person is one who measures by Dhamma and is pleased by Dhamma? Here, a certain person, seeing virtue, or seeing concentration, or seeing wisdom, taking that as a measure, generates confidence. This person is called one who measures by Dhamma and is pleased by Dhamma.

How is a person one who practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others? Here, a certain person is himself accomplished in virtue but does not encourage others to be accomplished in virtue; he is himself accomplished in concentration but does not encourage others to be accomplished in concentration; he is himself accomplished in wisdom but does not encourage others to be accomplished in wisdom; he is himself accomplished in liberation but does not encourage others to be accomplished in liberation; he is himself accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation but does not encourage others to be accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation. In this way, a person is one who practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others.

How is a person one who practices for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit? Here, a certain person is not himself accomplished in virtue but encourages others to be accomplished in virtue; he is not himself accomplished in concentration but encourages others to be accomplished in concentration; he is not himself accomplished in wisdom but encourages others to be accomplished in wisdom; he is not himself accomplished in liberation but encourages others to be accomplished in liberation; he is not himself accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation but encourages others to be accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation. In this way, a person is one who practices for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit.
163:
How is a person one who practices for both his own benefit and the benefit of others? Here, a certain person is himself accomplished in virtue and encourages others to be accomplished in virtue; he is himself accomplished in concentration and encourages others to be accomplished in concentration; he is himself accomplished in wisdom and encourages others to be accomplished in wisdom; he is himself accomplished in liberation and encourages others to be accomplished in liberation; he is himself accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation and encourages others to be accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation. In this way, a person is one who practices for both his own benefit and the benefit of others.

How is a person one who practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others? Here, a certain person is not himself accomplished in virtue and does not encourage others to be accomplished in virtue; he is not himself accomplished in concentration and does not encourage others to be accomplished in concentration; he is not himself accomplished in wisdom and does not encourage others to be accomplished in wisdom; he is not himself accomplished in liberation and does not encourage others to be accomplished in liberation; he is not himself accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation and does not encourage others to be accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation. In this way, a person is one who practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others.

How is a person one who torments himself, devoted to the practice of self-mortification? Here, a certain person is a naked ascetic, discarding conventions, licking his hands; he does not come when told "Come, venerable sir," he does not stop when told "Stop, venerable sir"; he does not accept food brought to him, or food specially prepared for him, or an invitation to a meal. He does not accept food from the rim of a pot, he does not accept food from the rim of a basket, he does not accept food across a threshold, he does not accept food across a stick, he does not accept food across a pestle, he does not accept food from two people eating together, he does not accept food from a pregnant woman, he does not accept food from a nursing woman, he does not accept food from a woman in the company of a man, he does not accept food from where food is being distributed, he does not accept food from where a dog is waiting, he does not accept food from where flies are swarming; he does not eat fish, he does not eat meat, he does not drink liquor, he does not drink wine, he does not drink fermented rice water. He is one who begs at only one house and subsists on one morsel, or he begs at two houses and subsists on two morsels ...pe... or he begs at seven houses and subsists on seven morsels. He subsists on one small saucer of food, or he subsists on two small saucers of food ...pe... or he subsists on seven small saucers of food. He takes food once a day, or once every two days ...pe... or once every seven days. In this way...
164:
He lives devoted to the practice of taking food at intervals of up to half a month. He is one who eats greens, or millet, or wild rice, or leather parings, or water-moss, or rice bran, or rice scum, or oil-cake, or grass, or cow dung; he subsists on forest roots and fruits, eating only fruits that have fallen of their own accord.

He wears garments of hemp, or hemp-mixed cloth, or shrouds, or refuse rags, or bark fibers, or antelope skins, or strips of antelope skin, or kusa-grass clothing, or bark clothing, or wood-shaving clothing, or a blanket of human hair, or a blanket of animal hair, or a garment of owl wings. He is one who plucks out hair and beard, devoted to the practice of plucking out hair and beard. He is one who stands continuously, rejecting seats. He is one who squats, devoted to the practice of squatting. He is one who lies on thorns, making his bed on thorns. He lives devoted to the practice of descending into water three times in the evening. Thus, in various ways, he lives devoted to the practice of tormenting and taxing the body. Such a person is called one who torments himself, devoted to the practice of self-torment.

And how is a person one who torments others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others? Here, a certain person is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs, a fowler, a hunter of wild animals, a cruel hunter, a fisherman, a thief, an executioner, a jailer, or others who follow such cruel occupations. Such a person is called one who torments others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others.

And how is a person one who torments both himself and others, devoted to the practice of tormenting both? Here, a certain person is an anointed Khattiya king or a wealthy Brāhmaṇa. Having had a new sacrificial hall built to the east of the city, having shaved off his hair and beard, having dressed in an antelope skin, and having [anointed] his body with ghee and oil...
165:
[The king], having anointed himself and scratching his back with a deer horn, enters the sacrificial hall together with his chief queen and the Brāhmaṇa chaplain. There he lies on the bare ground smeared with green grass. The king subsists on the milk from one teat of a cow that has a calf of similar appearance; the chief queen subsists on the milk from the second teat; the Brāhmaṇa chaplain subsists on the milk from the third teat; with the milk from the fourth teat, he makes an offering to the fire; and the calf subsists on the remainder. He says: 'Let this many bulls be slaughtered for the sacrifice; let this many steers be slaughtered for the sacrifice; let this many heifers be slaughtered for the sacrifice; let this many goats be slaughtered for the sacrifice; let this many sheep be slaughtered for the sacrifice; let this many trees be cut down for the sacrificial posts; let this many dabba-grasses be mown for the sacrificial grass.' And those who are his slaves, messengers, or workers, they perform their tasks weeping with tearful faces, being driven by the threat of punishment and the threat of fear. Thus, a person is one who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.

And how is a person one who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others? Such a person, tormenting neither himself nor others, dwells even in this life without hunger, extinguished, cooled, experiencing happiness, with a self that has become sublime.

In this Dispensation, a Tathāgata appears in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sublime One, a knower of the worlds, an incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. Having realized it for himself through direct knowledge, he makes known this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and Brāhmaṇas, its princes and people. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. A householder, or a householder's son, or one born into some other clan, hears that Dhamma...
166:
...or one who has been reborn hears it. Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. Possessed of that gain of faith, he reflects: "Household life is crowded, a path of dust; the life of homelessness is wide open. It is not easy for one living in a house to practice the holy life, which is perfectly complete, perfectly pure, and polished like a conch shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?" At a later time, abandoning a small or large mass of wealth, and abandoning a small or large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness.

Having thus gone forth, and being endowed with the training and livelihood of monks, he abandons the taking of life and abstains from the taking of life. With stick and weapon laid aside, he is conscientious, full of compassion, and dwells sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings.

He abandons the taking of what is not given and abstains from the taking of what is not given. He takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a self that is pure and free from theft.

He abandons unchastity and lives a holy life, dwelling apart, abstaining from the village practice of sexual intercourse.

He abandons false speech and abstains from false speech. He speaks the truth, is bound to the truth, is firm, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.

He abandons divisive speech and abstains from divisive speech. What he hears here he does not tell there to cause division among these people, and what he hears there he does not tell here to cause division among those people. Thus he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of those who are united. He loves concord, delights in concord, enjoys concord, and speaks words that create concord.

He abandons harsh speech and abstains from harsh speech. He speaks such words as are blameless, pleasing to the ear, lovely, reaching the heart, polite, liked by many, and agreeable to many.
167:
He abandons idle chatter and abstains from idle chatter. He speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks what is beneficial, speaks what is Dhamma, and speaks what is Vinaya. At the right time, he speaks words that are worth recording, accompanied by reasons, defined, and connected with the goal.

He abstains from damaging seeds and plants. He eats only one meal a day, abstaining from eating at night and outside the proper time. He abstains from watching dancing, singing, music, and theatrical shows. He abstains from wearing garlands, using perfumes, and beautifying the body with ointments. He abstains from high and large beds. He abstains from accepting gold and silver.

He abstains from accepting raw grain. He abstains from accepting raw meat. He abstains from accepting women and girls. He abstains from accepting male and female slaves. He abstains from accepting goats and sheep. He abstains from accepting poultry and pigs. He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. He abstains from accepting fields and land. He abstains from running errands and acting as a messenger. He abstains from buying and selling. He abstains from cheating with scales, coins, and measures. He abstains from bribery, deception, fraud, and trickery. He abstains from wounding, killing, binding, highway robbery, plundering, and violence.

He is content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to sustain his stomach. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. Just as a bird, wherever it flies, flies with only its wings as its burden, so too, a monk is content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to sustain his stomach. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself a blameless happiness.

On seeing a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and dejection might invade him, he practices for its restraint, he guards the eye faculty, and he achieves restraint of the eye faculty. On hearing a sound with the ear... [Pe]...
168:
Smelling an odor with the nose... [pe]... tasting a flavor with the tongue... [pe]... feeling a tangible object with the body... [pe]... cognizing a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the mind faculty (manindriya) unrestrained, evil unwholesome states of covetousness (abhijjhā) and distress (domanassa) might invade him, he practices for its restraint, he guards the mind faculty, and he achieves restraint of the mind faculty. Possessed of this noble restraint of the faculties (indriyasaṃvara), he experiences within himself an unblemished happiness.

He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside; he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, bowl, and other robes; he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, consuming, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating; he acts with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and remaining silent.

Possessed of this noble aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), this noble restraint of the faculties, this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension (satisampajañña), and this noble contentment (santuṭṭhi), he seeks out a secluded dwelling: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle grove, the open air, or a heap of straw. After returning from his almsround and having eaten his meal, he sits down, crossing his legs, keeping his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him. Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness. Having abandoned ill will (byāpāda) and malice, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will. Having abandoned sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha), he dwells free from sloth and torpor, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor. Having abandoned restlessness and remorse (uddhaccakukkucca), he dwells without agitation, with a mind inwardly stilled; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse. Having abandoned doubt (vicikicchā), he dwells having transcended doubt, not questioning 'how so?' concerning wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.

Having abandoned these five hindrances (nīvaraṇa), imperfections of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states...
169:
...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion (viveka). With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind (ekodibhāva), is without applied and sustained thought, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration (samādhi). With the fading away as well of rapture, he dwells equanimous (upekkhaka), mindful, and clearly comprehending, and he experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna of which the noble ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily.' With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it to the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa). He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion: 'There I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared here.' Thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings (cutūpapātañāṇa). With the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. He understands how beings pass on according to their kamma: 'These worthy beings who were ill-conducted in body, speech, and mind, revilers of noble ones, wrong in their views, giving effect to wrong view in their actions, on the dissolution of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell. But these worthy beings...'
170:
'They are endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind; they do not revile the Noble Ones; they hold right views and undertake actions based on right views. With the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. He understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliant, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavānaṃ khayañāṇa). He understands as it really is: 'This is suffering (dukkha)'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering (samudaya)'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering (nirodha)'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering (magga).' He understands as it really is: 'These are the taints (āsava)'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of the taints'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of the taints'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.' When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), from the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and from the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.' In this way, the person neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of torturing himself, nor does he torment others nor is he devoted to the practice of torturing others. Being neither a self-tormenter nor a foreign-tormenter, he dwells even in this life without hunger (craving), extinguished, cooled, experiencing happiness, with a self become divine.

Who is the person with lust (sarāga)? The person in whom lust is not abandoned is called a person with lust.

Who is the person with hatred (sadosa)? The person in whom hatred is not abandoned is called a person with hatred.

Who is the person with delusion (samoha)? The person in whom delusion is not abandoned is called a person with delusion.

Who is the person with pride (samāna)? The person in whom pride is not abandoned is called a person with pride.
171:
How does a person gain internal tranquility of mind (samatha) but not insight into higher wisdom (vipassanā)? Here, a certain person gains the attainments (samāpatti) of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere, but does not gain the supramundane path (magga) or fruition (phala). In this way, a person gains internal tranquility of mind but not insight into higher wisdom.

How does a person gain insight into higher wisdom but not internal tranquility of mind? Here, a certain person gains the supramundane path or fruition, but does not gain the attainments of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere. In this way, a person gains insight into higher wisdom but not internal tranquility of mind.

How does a person gain both internal tranquility of mind and insight into higher wisdom? Here, a certain person gains the attainments of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere, and also gains the supramundane path or fruition. In this way, a person gains both internal tranquility of mind and insight into higher wisdom.

How does a person gain neither internal tranquility of mind nor insight into higher wisdom? Here, a certain person gains neither the attainments of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere, nor the supramundane path or fruition. In this way, a person gains neither internal tranquility of mind nor insight into higher wisdom.

Who is the person who goes with the stream (anusotagāmī)? Here, a certain person indulges in sensual pleasures and performs unwholesome deeds. This person is called one who goes with the stream.

Who is the person who goes against the stream (paṭisotagāmī)? Here, a certain person does not indulge in sensual pleasures and does not perform unwholesome deeds. Even with pain and grief, with a tearful face and weeping, he leads the holy life (brahmacariya) that is perfectly complete and pure. This person is called one who goes against the stream.
172:
Who is the person of steadfast nature (ṭhitatto)? In this Teaching, a certain person, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is spontaneously reborn [in the Pure Abodes], there to attain final Nibbāna, not subject to return from that world. This person is called 'one of steadfast nature.'

Who is the Brahmin who has crossed over [the river of craving], reached the far shore [Nibbāna], and stands on dry land? In this Teaching, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself in this very life through direct knowledge. This person is called 'the Brahmin who has crossed over, reached the far shore, and stands on dry land.'

How is a person of little learning and not endowed with what has been heard? In this Teaching, a certain person has little learning in the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. That person, not knowing the meaning and not knowing the Dhamma of that little learning, does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma. Thus, a person is of little learning and not endowed with what has been heard.

How is a person of little learning but endowed with what has been heard? In this Teaching, a certain person has little learning in the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. That person, knowing the meaning and knowing the Dhamma of that little learning, practices in accordance with the Dhamma. Thus, a person is of little learning but endowed with what has been heard.

How is a person of great learning but not endowed with what has been heard? In this Teaching, a certain person has much learning in the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. That person, not knowing the meaning and not knowing the Dhamma of that great learning, does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma. Thus, a person is of great learning but not endowed with what has been heard.

How is a person of great learning and endowed with what has been heard? In this Teaching, a certain person has much learning in the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. That person, knowing the meaning and knowing the Dhamma of that great learning, practices in accordance with the Dhamma. Thus, a person is of great learning and endowed with what has been heard.
173:
Who is the unshakable ascetic (samaṇamacalo)? In this world, a certain person, with the destruction of the three fetters, is a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), not subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment. This person is called 'the unshakable ascetic.'

Who is the red lotus ascetic (samaṇapadumo)? In this world, a certain person, with the destruction of the three fetters and the thinning of greed, hatred, and delusion, is a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī), who comes back to this world only once more to make an end of suffering. This person is called 'the red lotus ascetic.'

Who is the white lotus ascetic (samaṇapuṇḍarīko)? In this world, a certain person, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is spontaneously reborn [in the Pure Abodes], there to attain final Nibbāna, not subject to return from that world. This person is called 'the white lotus ascetic.'

Who is the delicate ascetic among ascetics (samaṇasukhumālo)? In this world, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless fruit of mind and fruit of wisdom of Arahantship, having realized it for himself in this very life through direct knowledge. This person is called 'the delicate ascetic among ascetics.'

## Description of the Fours.

## 5. Designation of Five Types of Persons

Among those persons [mentioned in the summary], there is one who exerts himself in committing an offense and is remorseful [after committing it]. That person does not know, as it really is, the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom of Arahantship where those arisen evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder. To that person, it should be said: 'Venerable, taints born of committing an offense exist in you; taints born of remorse are increasing. It would be good if the venerable one, having abandoned the taints born of committing an offense and having dispelled the taints born of remorse, would develop the mind and wisdom. By developing thus, the venerable one will become equal to that fifth person.'

Among those persons, there is one who exerts himself in committing an offense but is not remorseful. That person does not know, as it really is, those arisen...
174:
He does not know as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom where those evil unwholesome states cease without remainder. He should be spoken to thus: "Friend, taints arising from transgression exist in you, but taints arising from remorse do not increase. It would be good if you, having abandoned the taints arising from transgression, would develop insight mind and insight wisdom. In this way, you will be equal to that fifth person."

Among those persons, one who does not commit a transgression but has remorse, does not know as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom where those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder. He should be spoken to thus: "Friend, taints arising from transgression do not exist in you, but taints arising from remorse increase. It would be good if you, having dispelled the taints arising from remorse, would develop insight mind and insight wisdom. In this way, you will be equal to that fifth person."

Among those persons, one who does not commit a transgression and has no remorse, does not know as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom where those evil unwholesome states cease without remainder. He should be spoken to thus: "Friend, taints arising from transgression do not exist in you, and taints arising from remorse do not increase. It would be good if you would develop insight mind and insight wisdom. In this way, you will be equal to that fifth person." These four persons, being thus exhorted and instructed by that fifth person, gradually reach the destruction of the taints.

And how does a person despise after giving? Here, a certain person gives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites to another person. To that giver, the thought occurs: "I give, and this one receives." Having given, he then despises that person. In this way, a person despises after giving.

And how does a person despise because of living together? Here, a certain person lives together with another person for two or three years. Because of living together, he then despises that person. In this way, a person despises because of living together.
175:
And how is a person easily led? Here, a certain person, when the praise or blame of another is being spoken, quickly becomes convinced. In this way, a person is easily led.

And how is a person fickle? Here, a certain person has temporary faith, temporary devotion, temporary love, and temporary confidence. In this way, a person is fickle.

And how is a person dull and deluded? Here, a certain person does not know wholesome and unwholesome states, does not know blameworthy and blameless states, does not know low and excellent states, and does not know states that are counterparts of dark and bright. In this way, a person is dull and deluded.

Among those, who are the five persons like warriors? The five warriors are: Here, a certain warrior, merely upon seeing a cloud of dust raised by soldiers, loses heart, falters, cannot steady himself, and is unable to enter the battlefield. Such a warrior is found in the world. This is the first warrior found existing in the world.

Furthermore, here, a certain warrior endures the cloud of dust, but merely upon seeing the array of banners on elephants, horses, or chariots, he loses heart, falters, cannot steady himself, and is unable to enter the battlefield. Such a warrior is found in the world. This is the second warrior found existing in the world.

Furthermore, here, a certain warrior endures the cloud of dust and endures the array of banners, but merely upon hearing the sound of shouting and marching, he loses heart, falters, cannot steady himself, and is unable to enter the battlefield. Such a warrior is found in the world. This is the third warrior found existing in the world.

Furthermore, here, a certain warrior endures the cloud of dust, endures the array of banners, and endures the shouting, but when he is struck and wounded in the clash of battle, he becomes exhausted and falls into despair. Such a warrior is found in the world. This is the fourth warrior found existing in the world.
176:
Furthermore, in this world, a certain warrior endures the cloud of dust, endures the array of banners, endures the shouting, and endures the clash of battle. Having conquered that battle, as a victor, he continues to occupy the very front of the battlefield. Such a warrior exists in this world. This is the fifth type of warrior found in the world. These five warriors are found in the world.

In the same way, these five persons similar to warriors are found among the monks. What five? Here, a certain monk, upon merely seeing a cloud of dust, loses heart, becomes dejected, cannot steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life; having manifested his weakness in the training, he disavows the training and returns to the lower life. What is the cloud of dust for him? Here, a monk hears: 'In such and such a village or town, there is a woman or a girl who is beautiful, attractive, graceful, and possessed of the most excellent complexion.' Having heard this, he loses heart, becomes dejected, cannot steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life; having manifested his weakness in the training, he disavows the training and returns to the lower life. This is the cloud of dust for him.

Just as that warrior, upon merely seeing a cloud of dust, loses heart, becomes dejected, cannot steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle, this person is just like that. Such a person exists among the monks. This is the first person similar to a warrior found among the monks.

Furthermore, here, a certain monk endures the cloud of dust, but upon merely seeing the array of banners, he loses heart, becomes dejected, cannot steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life; having manifested his weakness in the training, he disavows the training and returns to the lower life. What is the array of banners for him? Here, a monk does not merely hear: 'In such and such a village or town, there is a woman or a girl who is beautiful, attractive, graceful, and possessed of the most excellent complexion.' Rather, he himself sees the woman or girl who is beautiful, attractive, graceful, and possessed of the most excellent complexion. Having seen her, he loses heart, becomes dejected, cannot steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life; having manifested his weakness in the training, he disavows the training and returns to the lower life. This is the array of banners for him.
177:
Just as that warrior endures the cloud of dust, but upon merely seeing the array of banners, he loses heart, becomes dejected, cannot steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle, this person is just like that. Such a person exists among the monks. This is the second person similar to a warrior found among the monks.

Furthermore, here, a certain monk endures the cloud of dust and endures the array of banners, but upon merely hearing the sound of shouting, he loses heart, becomes dejected, cannot steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life; having manifested his weakness in the training, he disavows the training and returns to the lower life. What is the sound of shouting for him? Here, a woman approaches a monk who has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, and she smiles, talks, laughs loudly, and teases him. Being smiled at, talked to, laughed at, and teased by the woman, he loses heart, becomes dejected, cannot steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life; having manifested his weakness in the training, he disavows the training and returns to the lower life. This is the sound of shouting for him.

Just as that warrior endures the cloud of dust and endures the array of banners, but upon merely hearing the sound of shouting, he loses heart, becomes dejected, cannot steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle, this person is just like that. Such a person exists among the monks. This is the third person similar to a warrior found among the monks.

Furthermore, here, a certain monk endures the cloud of dust, endures the array of banners, and endures the sound of shouting, but in the clash of battle, he is struck down and meets with ruin. What is the clash of battle for him? Here, a woman approaches a monk who has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, and she sits down near him, lies down near him, and overwhelms him. Being sat near, lied near, and overwhelmed by the woman, he engages in sexual intercourse without disavowing the training and without manifesting his weakness. This is the clash of battle for him.

Just as that warrior endures the cloud of dust, endures the array of banners, and endures the sound of shouting, but in the clash of battle, he is struck down and meets with ruin,
178:
This person is like that warrior. In this Teaching, there is such a person. This is the fourth person like a warrior who is found existing among the bhikkhus.

Furthermore, in this Teaching, a certain bhikkhu endures the cloud of dust, endures the array of banners, endures the battle-cry, and endures the clash of arms. Having conquered that battle, as a victorious warrior, he remains at the very front of that battlefield. What is that bhikkhu's victory in battle? In this Teaching, a woman approaches a bhikkhu who has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut; she sits down close to him, lies down close to him, and overwhelms him. When he is being sat near, lain near, and overwhelmed by that woman, he disentangles himself, frees himself, and goes wherever he wishes.

He resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle grove, the open air, or a heap of straw. Having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, he sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him. Having abandoned covetousness (abhijjhā) for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind from covetousness. Having abandoned ill-will (byāpāda), he dwells with a mind free from ill-will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill-will. Having abandoned sloth and torpor (thina-middha), he dwells free from sloth and torpor, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind from sloth and torpor. Having abandoned restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), he dwells without agitation, with a mind inwardly stilled; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Having abandoned doubt (vicikicchā), he dwells having transcended doubt, without perplexity regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind from doubt.

Having abandoned these five hindrances (nīvaraṇa), which are defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna... (Pe)... the third jhāna... (Pe)... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, pliant, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsava). He understands as it really is: 'This is suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.' He understands as it really is: 'These are the taints'; he understands as it really is: 'This is...
179:
...the origin of the taints'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of the taints'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.'

When he knows thus and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), liberated from the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and liberated from the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.' This is his victory in the battlefield. Just as that warrior endures the cloud of dust, endures the array of banners, endures the battle-cry, and endures the clash of arms, and having conquered that battle, as a victorious warrior, remains at the very front of that battlefield; so too is this person like that warrior. In this Teaching, there is such a person. This is the fifth person like a warrior who is found existing among the bhikkhus. These five persons like warriors are found existing among the bhikkhus.

Among them, who are the five types of alms-round practitioners (piṇḍapātika)? One is an alms-round practitioner because of foolishness and extreme delusion. One is an alms-round practitioner because of evil desires and being overwhelmed by evil desires. One is an alms-round practitioner because of madness and a distracted mind. One is an alms-round practitioner thinking, 'This is praised by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.'
